# Foreword

It is a meaningful endeavor to compile the 10-year journey of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) into a single book, and I believe this is significant not only for me but also for all citizens.

Every nation has its own historical philosophy (歷史哲學) to guide its path, but we have initiated the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) to seek a faster and more substantial way to create history. Although the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) has only been around for 10 years, through it, we have found methods to wash away the dark aspects of our past and cultivated the confidence to actively challenge the future and realize our ambitious ideals.

The popularization of the will to "do it" has brought about a revolutionary change in the national lifestyle, and the national awareness that "we can also live well" has not only dispelled the long-held notion of accepting poverty and trials as fate but also instilled in us the courage to overcome all obstacles before us through the firm belief in the power of unity, solidarity, and cooperation.

While it is often said that history flows by, I believe that history is not something that merely passes but is created by the people living in that era. This is because history and humanity are not separate concepts but are inseparably connected, like the two wheels of a vehicle. The existence of humanity without history is meaningless, and history without humanity is even more empty. Reflecting on this, we realize the immense significance of human existence in shaping the era they live in.

How the history of the past is illuminated today serves as a clear measure of how the protagonists of history have lived. We have clearly declared our national resolve to strive for the creation of values that must be projected into the future, while reflecting more accurately on the past through the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement).


--- (p. 6) ---

We have been able to be proud of our ancestors and make our descendants proud by building an era where we can firmly establish the foundation for a new age that can sprout within, and outside, we have solidified the foundation of self-reliance that can calmly face any competition. There has never been a time in history, past or present, East or West, where the outcome of history has been purely accidental. If we cannot deny the historical logic that an era can only unfold brightly when the national character of that time is proactive, then we cannot afford to relax our previous progressive attitude for any reason. The Saemaul Undong in the 1980s must be further activated to respond to the national goal of building a democratic welfare society. If our resolve and determination to pioneer the future must be renewed, we must retrace our steps over the past 10 years and exercise wisdom to learn from strengths and make up for weaknesses in order to continue our substantial progress. Although this 10-year history compiled this time may not be perfect, I believe it can serve as a double-sided mirror reflecting the past and the future. I expect all citizens to widely utilize this book as a companion in your daily lives. Finally, I would like to express my deepest gratitude to the authors and editorial committee members who have devoted their heart and soul to compiling this book.

November 30, 1980

Minister of Home Affairs, Seo Jeong-hwa (徐廷和)


--- (p. 7) ---

# Preface

Editor-in-Chief Kim Yu-Hyuk (金裕赫)

To chronicle the first decade of the Saemaul Undong (運動), we present this 10-year history.
History (歷史) flows like a great river (大河), connecting past and present, but it is clear that those living in an era shape its direction (方向).
We have struggled to pursue a brighter tomorrow (來日) by critically reflecting on our past history (歷史) more than ever before.
However, the circumstances (與件) surrounding us did not always align (造成) with our perspective (立場) in a lenient (寬容) direction (方向).
The relentless trials (試鍊) we faced, harsh as they were, drove us into despair (絶望) and disillusionment (失意), yet our persistent efforts (努力) to overcome these challenges always carried an active (積極性) spirit within restraint (忍人自重).
The proactive (積極性) spirit (脈絡) that has continued (連綿) with our national history (民族史) not only gave birth to the Saemaul Undong (運動) but also manifested as a resolve (決意) to wash away the historical (歷史的) burdens (煩惱) from our concrete (具體的) lives (生活部面).
Though we once viewed the future (未來), nature (自然), and fate (運命) as a single object (對象) of terror (恐怖), we have reached a stage where we seek (追求) infinite (無限) possibilities (可能性) within the future (未來), learn (眞理) the truth (見仁得仁) from nature (自然), and re-establish (再定立) our traditional (在來) fate (運命觀) as self-determination (自我決定論).
We have not only transformed (變革) our living systems (生活體系) through proactive (能動的) attitudes (態度) that challenge (挑戰) conventions (因襲), such as altering (位置) the location (位置) and structure (構造) of villages that were once considered (名堂視) auspicious (名堂視) and removing (脫) the thatched roofs (草家) of houses passed down (累代) through generations, but also constructed (建設) markets (市場) and roads (道路) for circulation (流通) by cutting through (切開) the spine (脊椎) of the village's rear mountain (山), where vital energy (精氣) was believed to flow (流).
The pains (提起) arising from the challenges (挑戰) to conventions (因襲) and the struggles (精進) of self-reform (自己改革) were many.


--- (p. 8) ---

However, the value of the hot sweat was not in vain, and the foundation was laid for the modernization of rural villages (몰촌) and people's living society (민衆生活社會) to be able to run on the track of modernization (近代化).

In particular, history (歷史) is not only determined by its developed results (結果), but the process (過程) by which it was achieved should be more emphasized.

The 10-year history (10年史) of Saemaul Undong (述励) is a comprehensive (綜合的) account of how the Saemaul tree has grown, what the taste of the fruits it bears is like, and how well its roots have taken hold.

Of course, it is not possible to include all the developments (發展狀況) over the 10 years (10年間) in the limited space (紙面), but in order to leave out nothing, no matter how small, this compilation (編基) project (事業) was carried out with the wide participation (參與) of experts (人士) from various fields (分野).

There were many difficulties (隘路) in promoting the project (事業推進), but thanks to the active cooperation (協力) of the participating members (參與人士), we were able to publish the 10-year history (10年史) in two volumes: a general overview (總論篇) and a data volume (資料篇). Moreover, to make it useful for foreigners (外國人), an English summary (英文要約書) was included as an appendix (附錄) to the general overview (總論篇), and important statistical data (統計資料) in the data volume (資料篇) were edited with English terms (英文語彙).

We hope that this book (册) will be widely used (活用) both domestically and internationally (中外) and become a stepping stone for building a more fruitful second decade (10年代). We also hope that any data (資料) not included here will be supplemented (補完) and published (續刊) in the future. With these hopes, we gather the thoughts of all those involved (人士諸位) and present this preface (序).

# Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

## Section 1: Preface

On April 22, 1970, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), first proposed by President Park Chung-hee at the National Conference of Local Governors (全國地方長官會議), reached its 10th anniversary.
As the old saying goes, "In ten years, even mountains and rivers change," but in the 10 years of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), our country's landscape changed remarkably.
The old saying about mountains and rivers changing refers to natural changes, such as rain and snow causing erosion on mountains and altering the courses of streams. However, the changes in our landscape over the 10 years of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) were not merely natural.
Rather, they were the result of our people's deliberate and intentional pursuit of goals, challenging nature. Therefore, the social changes achieved through the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) were a development aimed at fulfilling our people's desire to live better. At the same time, it signifies a pioneering historical meaning that seeks to break away from a complacent attitude and create a new foundation for life.
To be frank, our people have a long history of 5,000 years to boast of, but we did not have a distinct historical chapter of actively challenging nature and achieving pioneering feats.
In some respects, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) can be seen as an expression of an active attitude that seeks new possibilities within nature while harboring dreams for the future and revising the fatalism we had held onto.
This is because, for a long time, we preferred ease over adventure, valued the beauty of submission over resistance, and emphasized passive endurance over active perseverance, given the frequent external threats and internal troubles we faced.


--- (p. 16) ---

The spirit of perseverance based on endurance can be considered from two aspects. One is endurance that presupposes tranquility and ease, while the other is endurance that arises from pursuing development through adventurous challenges and trials. The Saemaul Undong clearly embodies the latter character and meaning.

Looking back, for our people, the most feared objects were the future, nature, and fate. Our view of the future had no guarantees, and challenging a future without guarantees was considered reckless. This led to a general tendency to return to the past to alleviate present dissatisfaction, resulting in a passive attitude towards life. Therefore, the future was difficult to interpret as anything beyond the experiences of the past.

Nature was always a direct object of fear, making it difficult to escape the preconceived notion that it was inhabited by gods. There was also a vague expectation that nature, through its natural order, would protect submissive humans, making it difficult to reject the polytheistic belief of "gods everywhere."

The fate of humans was considered innate and predestined, with the notion that harmony within this predestination was the essence of human existence, life, and one's lifetime. This led to a belief that human fate was predetermined rather than something to be pioneered, further deepening the general passive and receptive attitude towards life.

However, we began to feel that we could no longer hesitate in such a state, stimulated by internal and external factors. Externally, the international environment was changing with the fierce rise of the principle of competition, while internally, we could no longer afford to sit back and enjoy comfort in a state of poverty and trials.


--- (p. 17) ---

## Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

We began to realize our own potential. Here, we started to reflect on our past mistakes and began to truly appreciate the experiences and lessons of others. Our declaration that we too could live well was, to put it clearly, an expression of self-aware will and an active attitude. We strongly resisted the resignation that had been in our hearts and, through repeated self-reflection, overcame our passive attitudes. We made a firm national decision to find a path to new prosperity without hesitation.

To achieve the two supreme goals of development and security, we strove to find the basis for possibility in our current situation. As a result, we realized that to build a foundation for development, we needed to find a Korean model for economic development. Similarly, to build a foundation for security, we had to strengthen our self-defense capabilities.

As historians have noted, since the founding of Goryeo (918 AD), we have faced nearly 100 invasions and challenges from other nations. Our impoverished lives were a result of the powerlessness that stemmed from this history. Moreover, the loss of our self-defense capabilities, which was a consequence of this powerlessness, only exacerbated the trials of war.

However, we did not neglect to study how to live wisely in that era. On one hand, we established and promoted economic development plans to create a foundation for development. On the other hand, as guardians of peace, we participated in the Vietnam War, contributing to the common prosperity of humanity and proclaiming our will without reservation.

The most important shortcut to awakening human potential and fostering an active attitude is to set achievable goals.

We, who were steeped in poverty and trials, were like travelers who had collapsed in the desert, exhausted from hunger, thirst, and the scorching sun, waiting for death. However, the presentation of development goals—through economic development plans—that we could achieve in five or ten years, allowing us to live as well as anyone else, was like an oasis in the desert.


--- (p. 18) ---

To the traveler who had collapsed, it threw a hope like the news that an "oasis" was 50 meters ahead, giving them a sense of meaning.

With all our might, we ran towards the "oasis" just like that traveler, repeatedly enduring and enduring towards our goal. As a result, we left behind footsteps of development that were significant enough to attract global attention.

On the other hand, the experience of participating in the foreign battlefield contributed to the enhancement of our international status and increased our speaking rights in the international community. It also gave many young people an international perspective and the confidence to defeat any enemy, no matter the situation. This boosted national morale, expanding the possibility of suppressing the enemy's aggressive ambitions with an unstoppable momentum.

For over a thousand years since the founding of Korea, we had to endure the nightmare of war every seven years on average. However, for nearly 30 years, albeit imperfect, we have maintained an unprecedented long-term peace.

The continuation of this peaceful state allowed us to repeatedly develop in terms of construction, and the sustained attitude of development helped us build a secure foundation in terms of security.

From this perspective, the Saemaul Undong contributed significantly as a new impetus for historical development, and its meaning cannot be underestimated.

A nation that lives without reflecting on its history cannot guarantee its future, as it lacks a philosophy that looks towards the future.

Every nation's history has two common aspects: one is the bright side of history, and the other is the dark side. The bright side of history is indeed something to be proud of, as it instills high pride and confidence. However, the dark side of history also provides valuable lessons that stimulate self-reflection.

Therefore, the value obtained from hiding a shameful history is less than the greater developmental energy found when using the lessons from that history as a stimulus for national awakening.


--- (p. 19) ---

## Section 2: Historical Significance of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

### 1. Retrospect on National History

The national historical significance and achievements of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) and how future historians will evaluate them are matters of great interest. However, no one can deny that it served as a driving force for rapid growth during Korea's modernization efforts in the 1970s and became the seed of a spiritual revolution.

First, let us consider our geopolitical situation. As a peninsula jutting out into Northeast Asia, Korea is connected to China and Siberia to the north and is close to Japan across the sea to the south. Situated between the southward-expanding and northward-advancing forces, the Korean Peninsula has always been under the threat and crisis of war, with no peace to be found. The task of maintaining independence and unity while preserving a single ethnicity, culture, and nation in the dynamic interplay of power among great nations is both meaningful and arduous.

With a strong consciousness of independence beating in our hearts, we have managed to maintain our sovereignty despite numerous foreign invasions throughout history. Without a strong sense of national pride and mission, we might have been annexed by a great power long ago. Thanks to the appearance of great patriots and the wise responses of the people during times of national crisis, we have been able to steer our fate, like a candle in the wind, to the present day.

While grounding ourselves in this strong spiritual independence, we have had to live with poverty as if it were our destiny. Our land is narrow, and our population is excessive. Moreover, we lacked resources and technological development. Agriculture


--- (p. 20) ---

Outside industries did not exist, so many people were tied to the land. Strong attachment to farmland and family and clan groups centered around it had connected production and life. While advanced nations had already established the foundations of modernization through Enlightenment ideas and the Industrial Revolution, forming the basis of nation-state formation, we had not achieved either the spiritual awareness or practical achievements necessary for modernization, falling behind in the process.

In the mid-Joseon period, some practical scholars had planted the seeds of productive ideas and technology, but there was no class to take responsibility for them, nor any group to lead them. Moreover, there were no resources or science to connect them to an industrial revolution. In this process, some enlightened intellectuals initiated the Gwanghwamun Movement in response to foreign invasions, but they faced strong resistance from conservative forces. The Donghak Peasant Revolution also emerged but ultimately failed. In the end, no force or group could lead our modernization, leaving us as a backward nation. We then experienced 36 years of colonial rule by Japan, which had risen as a modern industrial power aiming for national prosperity and military strength.

The strong national consciousness preserved during the long colonial rule erupted in resistance against Japanese rule, but national unity was insufficient, and we lacked the political and economic power to end their rule ourselves. Thus, we welcomed liberation in 1945. However, this liberation was achieved without our own national strength for independence and unification, relying instead on the balance of power among great nations. Our fate was not in our own hands. The power vacuum left by Japan's defeat was filled by the U.S. and the Soviet Union, whose post-World War II temporary cooling period was fundamentally driven by their national interests—the U.S.'s East Asia policy and the Soviet Union's southward expansion policy. The result was the stark reality of national division, a consequence of our failure to pursue national unity and reunification with proactive will and effort, stemming from both our internal lack of capacity for self-determination and the external influence of great powers.


--- (p. 21) ---

# Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

The division of our nation and country was realized by the force of the Cold War. In their Cold War system, we did not have the leeway to deviate from its orbit, which resulted in the tragedy of fratricidal war known as the 6.25 conflict.
The wounds of the post-war period were so deep that the reconstruction after the war brought us many trials. Extreme economic chaos and political disorder led to the events of April 19 and May 16.

## 2. The Industrial Revolution: The Starting Point of Modernization

The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) was a great leap forward for our nation, a movement in which all citizens participated for the first time in our history. Many countries around the world have openly expressed their astonishment and envy of the planning, organization, leadership, drive, and achievements of our Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement).
As is widely known, the world powers led by Britain rushed to promote the Industrial Revolution to create wealthy and powerful modern nations, thus achieving early advancement as advanced countries.
However, the starting period of our modernization was about 200 years later than Britain, 150 years later than Germany, and about 100 years later than Japan. We were, so to speak, placed in a time lag.
We had to rid ourselves of poverty and become a prosperous nation once and for all. From the 1960s onwards, we focused on economic development to cultivate our national strength, so that we could overcome the insecurity and crises of war and become a nation that could live in peace.
Our plan started almost from scratch. All we had was the resolve, ambition, and action to become a nation that could live proudly and to build a strong and proud country. We believed that production and exports were the way to escape poverty and prevent war, and we united as one with the leaders at the center to realize this path. Thus, we built factories, paved expressways, constructed ports, and created reservoirs.
We began to exert our united strength to create the "Miracle of the Han River" on this land, aiming to replicate the "Miracle of the Rhine" achieved by post-war Germany.


--- (p. 22) ---

It was.
This further accelerated in the 1970s, and the Saemaul Undong (運動) served as a catalyst for this acceleration. With the Saemaul spirit, we initiated the Saemaul Undong in rural areas and, building on its success, expanded the experience and confidence gained to factories and cities.
Thus, despite the crises of 1973, such as the fluctuations in oil (石油) and food (食糧) resources that led to a global economic slowdown, we were able to overcome these trials and achieve continuous growth.
Industrialization (工業化) and urbanization (都市化) further progressed. Our total national production (國民生産) increased remarkably, and all citizens improved and enhanced their lives through the Saemaul spirit of diligence (勤勉), self-help (自助), and cooperation (協同). This total development (發展) of the national economy (國家經濟) led to a revolution (革命) in the lives of the people (國民生活). This was the Korean industrial revolution (産業革命) that began in our generation, fulfilling the unfinished industrial revolution of our ancestors (祖上) and serving as the starting signal for the modernization (近代化) of our homeland (祖國).
We have now reached the point where we can draw a new chapter in the history (歷史) of a modern nation (近代國家) based on the foundation of the national economy (國民經濟).

### 3. Prelude to Establishing the Substantial Foundation for Democratization (民主化)

The substantial realization (具現) of democracy (民主主義) requires a high level of economic (經濟的) growth and stability, as well as a high level of political (政治的) and intellectual (知的) awareness among the people (國民). Without these, democracy (民主主義) would be merely formal or institutional imitation, lacking substance (內實).
We must not forget that the maturity (成熟) of British democracy (民主主義) today is based on a solid economic (經濟的) foundation achieved through industrialization (産業化).
Economic growth (經濟成長) and stability are necessary for the political consciousness (政治意識) of the people (國民) to become rational and for their political behavior (政治行態) to foster compromise (妥協) and harmony (調和).
The fact that the political (政治) and social (社會) instability in France for a long time stemmed from the hasty pursuit of political development (政治發展) without an economic (經濟的) foundation of growth (成長) or stability (安定) serves as a very important lesson (敎訓) for us.
How should we prioritize (優先順位) political (政治的) democratization (民主化) or economic (經濟的) industrialization (産業化)?


--- (p. 23) ---

The problem at hand must be decided very wisely and carefully, taking into account the historical (歷史的) traditions (傳統) and real (現實的) conditions (與件) that the country possesses.

The Saemaul Undong (運動) is an industrialization (產業化) movement (運動) to promote our economic development (經濟發展) efficiently (能率的), organizationally (組織的), and rapidly (加速的). We believe that through this industrialization (產業化), we can establish a political order (政治秩序) of compromise (妥協), harmony (調和), stability (安定), and peace (平和) progressively (漸進的) on the economic (經濟的) foundation (基盤).

In other words, our ideal (理想) was to avoid repeating the vicious cycle (惡循環) of revolution (革命) caused by prioritizing democratization (民主化) over industrialization (產業化), as seen in France, and to achieve economic development (經濟發展) through industrialization (產業化) like the United Kingdom (英國), and further, to accomplish peaceful (平和的) political transition (政權交替) and political climate (政治風土).

We have learned through much experience (經驗) that political development (政治發展) is not a product (產物) of political manipulation (操作), but a historical (歷史) product (產物) resulting from economic (經濟的), social (社會的), and cultural (文化的) conclusions (歸結).

We believe that such empirical (經驗的) facts (事實) should become very precious (所重) experiences (經驗) for future political development (政治發展). This is because the 2,000-year (餘年) long ideological (思想) background (背景) for democracy (民主主義) and the 200-year (餘年) process (過程) of realizing democracy (民主主義) in Western European democratic culture (西歐民主文化) sufficiently (充分) explain (說明) it.

## 4. Saemaul Undong (運動) is a movement (運動) to reduce regional (地域) gaps (隔差)

The most pressing issue (當面課題) that we must all address together is the economic (經濟) problem. Such economic (經濟) problems must include issues of production (生產), distribution (分配), and consumption (消費).

No one can raise an objection (異議) to the fact that the achievements (成果) of the industrialization (產業化) and industrialization (工業化) we have promoted since the 1960s (年代) have brought remarkable development (發展) to the gross national product (國民總生產) in terms of total quantity (總量的). It is true that our national power (國力) has increased (增强) and the lives (生活) of individual (個個) citizens (國民) have become more prosperous (風豊) and improved (向上). In other words, we have all escaped from absolute (絶對的) poverty (貧困). However, this did not mean that all our economic (經濟) problems were solved.

In the process (過程) of economic growth (經濟成長), we found that in our pursuit (企圖) of efficiency (能率化) and speed (迅速化), many economic (經濟的) and social (社會的) side effects (副作用) had unintentionally (意圖) arisen. These were the gaps (隔差), disconnections (斷絕), and the social (社會) and cultural (文化的) issues that arose from them.


--- (p. 24) ---

# It was a problem of restructuring.

That is, the gap between industries, classes, and regions had become a serious social problem. Ideally, we should solve these problems simultaneously. However, that is impossible. Because the human and material constraints are too great for us to solve them all at once. While deeply recognizing the inevitability that we must solve these problems ourselves, we hesitate to decide on simultaneous solutions due to economic immaturity.

However, the most basic and urgent problem we had to solve was the regional gap between urban and rural areas.

Industrialization and urbanization had rapidly progressed, and farmers moved to cities seeking higher economic income and a more comfortable life. As a result, both urban and rural areas began to face their own social problems.

An income gap emerged between urban and rural areas, leading to differences in the quality of life. It was only natural that this created a sense of alienation among the people.

To reduce the gap between rural and urban areas and improve the quality and aspects of rural life to urban standards, we had to modernize the countryside. This led to the emergence of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) as a rural modernization movement.

We needed to research strategies and techniques for rural modernization. That was precisely the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement).

Roads were paved, roofs were repaired, bridges were built, and walls were mended. The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) successfully improved the living environment in rural areas. Through this process, farmers came to believe that if they were diligent, self-reliant, and cooperative, "we can live well."

With the confidence that "we can also live well," we found the motivation to improve. Through the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), we realized that we could improve the environment, enhance our lives, and enjoy culture. We all became more diligent, saved more, and planned our lives more carefully.

In this sense, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) was indeed a spiritual revolution that instilled courage and confidence in farmers.


--- (p. 25) ---

# Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) began as a movement for better living, but it gradually expanded and deepened into a movement aimed at improving living environments, reforming consciousness structures, increasing income, and reducing regional disparities.

## 5. The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) as a Multipurpose Comprehensive Development Movement

The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) was initiated in rural areas with farmers as the main driving force, aiming to modernize the countryside and reduce the gap between urban and rural areas.

Farmers have a strong attachment to land, as it is the basis of their lives and production, and the place where their ancestors are buried. Through blood ties, geographical ties, and emotional bonds centered around the land, they have maintained a communal way of life for generations. This is how the simple patriotism of farmers and their sense of shared feelings have grown. This is the origin of farmers' nationalist consciousness.

Deep within the hearts of our people lies such a nationalist consciousness, which can be attributed to both our geopolitical conditions and our historical experiences. The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) can be said to have ignited the deep-seated consciousness of farmers.

Without the farmers' love for their hometowns and their country, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) would never have spread and deepened. It was this love that enabled the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) to demonstrate remarkable potential.

Through the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), the hearts of the people have been stirred, and through the process of the movement, they have gained numerous experiences and firm beliefs.

Thus, the flames of the movement have spread to cities, factories, workplaces, and schools, both consciously and unconsciously, forming a shared sphere of living and production. Therefore, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) became a symbol of Korea's modernization in the 1970s and laid the foundation for the lives of the people. To that extent, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) began to take root deeply in our consciousness and lives.

As in our long history, when the entire nation united with fervent passion and solid cooperation for the modernization and strong nation-building of the country,


--- (p. 26) ---

There had never been such a precedent of dedication.
Such national unity and hard work would not be in vain, and we have achieved our long-awaited goal of $100 billion in exports ahead of schedule, and we have accomplished a national income of $1,000 per capita ahead of schedule. We have also produced 41 million bushels of grain, achieving self-sufficiency in our main staple food. In achieving these goals ahead of the target year, the spiritual foundation provided by the Saemaul Undong (運動) was undoubtedly a great support, which is beyond any further discussion.
Truly, our generation living today has become proud to have been a great force in the modernization of our homeland through the Saemaul Undong (運動).
The Saemaul Undong (運動) spread without discrimination of region, class, workplace, age, or gender, and the spirit of Saemaul permeated all aspects of the people's lives, becoming the spiritual driving force for national development.
If the Saemaul Undong (運動) of the 1970s was about improving the quality of national life through increased material production, then the Saemaul Undong (運動) of the 1980s can be said to have its significance in developing the qualitative content of national life as a spiritual revolution movement. Thus, the Saemaul Undong (運動) aims to build a new society in harmony with these two aspects, so that we can all realize a meaningful life.

### Section 3: The Korean People (韓民族) and Korean History (韓國史)

#### 1. The Origin of the Korean People (韓民族)

There are generally two views on the origin of the Korean people (韓民族): the Southern Origin Theory (南方起源說) and the Northern Origin Theory (北方起源說).
The Southern Origin Theory (南方起源說) is supported by archaeological evidence, such as the single-edged axe. This tool, used in Southeast Asia (東南亞) and Polynesia, is also found in the Ryukyu Islands (琉球列島) and northern Kyushu (北九州), and has spread to the Korean Peninsula (韓半島). Additionally, ethnological evidence includes tattooing (文身) and grass burial (草葬), which are indeed southern tools or customs. However, their numbers are small, and such phenomena can only be found south of the Han River (漢江). This is precisely the difficulty with the Southern Origin Theory (南方起源說).


--- (p. 27) ---

# Chapter 1 (第1章) Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (新村運動)

The difficulties of the Southern Origin Theory (南方起源說) ultimately strongly suggest that the Korean people (韓民族) originated from the northern region (北方). This is also sufficiently supported linguistically (言語學) and archaeologically (考古學的).

The Korean language (韓國語) is a branch of the Altaic languages (語) that originated from the Buyeo (夫餘) and Hanjo (韓祖語) language families, and it is said to have a kinship relationship (親族關係) with Turkish, Mongol, and Tungusic languages (語). The Buyeo language family (夫餘系) developed into the language of Goguryeo (高句麗語), while the Han language family (韓系) evolved into the languages of Silla (新羅語) and Baekje (百濟語). Additionally, one branch of the Buyeo language (夫餘語) crossed the sea to form the foundation of the Japanese language (日本語).

In this context, the languages of the Three Kingdoms period (三國時代) maintained close relationships, with Silla (新羅語) and Baekje (百濟語) being particularly similar, although they did not use the same language. The unification of languages (言語) began in the mid-7th century with the unification of the Three Kingdoms (三國統一) as a catalyst (契機). From this period, the language of the Gyeongju region (慶州地方), Silla (新羅語), became central, absorbing Baekje (百濟語) and Goguryeo (高句麗語) languages, and evolving into the ancient Korean language (韓國語).

Not only are the linguistic systems (系統) connected to the northern region (北方), but prehistoric artifacts (先史時代의 遺物) also trace back to the north (北方).

The use of stone tools (石器) and pottery (土器) characterizes the Neolithic people (新石器人) who appeared in the Korean Peninsula (韓半島) around 4,000 B.C. These earliest Neolithic people (新石器人) used undecorated pottery (無文土器), which is believed to be connected to the Siberian lineage (系統).

The representative pottery (土器) of the Neolithic Age (新石器時代), comb-patterned pottery (櫛文土器), began to be used by people across the country (全國) around 3,000 B.C.

The relationship between the Bronze Age people (靑銅器人)(無文土器人) and the Neolithic people (新石器人)(櫛文土器人) is unclear. However, undecorated pottery (無文土器) sites and comb-patterned pottery (櫛文土器) sites are distinctly different, even when located close to each other. This fact suggests that the two ethnic groups (人種) lived under different living conditions (生活條件) and had racial differences (種族上).

The undecorated pottery people (無文土器人) were not only armed with bronze tools (靑銅器) but also had stable food supplies (食糧供給) through agriculture (農耕). Therefore, they could easily absorb, assimilate, or exterminate the comb-patterned pottery people (櫛文土器人), who were numerically inferior (數的) and still in the foraging economic stage (採集經濟).

These Bronze Age people (靑銅器人)(無文土器人) are likely the Ye-Maek (穢貊)(or Ye (濊) and Maek (貊)), Han (韓), and other Dongyi tribes (東夷族) mentioned in ancient Chinese texts (古文獻). They likely absorbed or assimilated other groups through


--- (p. 28) ---

The remnants of the Neolithic people (comb-pattern pottery people) are estimated to be Paleo Asiatics. In other words, the Korean people are believed to have been formed by the absorption, assimilation, or expulsion of the Neolithic people (comb-pattern pottery people), Paleo Asiatics, by the Bronze Age people (plain pottery people, Dongyi people) who migrated southward, with some southern elements added, leading to the present day.

## 2. Growth of the Korean People

After the Dongyi people entered Manchuria and the Korean Peninsula, they grew relatively smoothly as a nation. There were no major migrations or significant intermingling with other nations, and they lived as a community bound by the same blood and culture in the same region.

However, nations were not formed from the prehistoric era. They were gradually formed with the development of society. In the tribal society, people only grew as a race. However, the numerous tribes that formed the race were the seeds that would later form the nation. Through the city-state era, the earliest form of the state, the tribes began to unite. This was the beginning of the formation of a nation.

Thus, numerous city-states merged into 5-6 federated kingdoms, which then merged into Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla, competing with each other, and the spirit of unification matured during this time. Until then, the Dongyi people's sphere of activity was mainly south of the Yalu River and the Songhua River, including Manchuria and the Korean Peninsula.

By the mid-7th century, the competition among the Three Kingdoms ended, and unification was achieved by Silla. Of course, it was not perfect. The Manchurian region, which had been the sphere of activity of the Three Kingdoms, was excluded from its territory, and the remnants of Goguryeo established Balhae there. Therefore, Silla actually only unified the Korean Peninsula, and that too, only south of the Taedong River and the Wonsan Bay line.

Nevertheless, Silla's unification of the peninsula had significant historical meaning. Above all, it laid the foundation for the formation of the Korean people on an independent basis. Although Unified Silla and Balhae formed a North-South States situation and the two countries were in opposition, the territory and residents of Unified Silla,...


--- (p. 29) ---

## Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

Thus, their society, language, and culture came to form the mainstream of Korean history. In this regard, the unification of the Three Kingdoms by Silla holds significant meaning in national history.

Silla was the last among the Three Kingdoms to establish an ancient state system. While Goguryeo had been organizing its ancient state system since around A.D. 1, and Baekje since around A.D. 3, Silla began this process around A.D. 3 as well.

Why was Silla able to become the protagonist of unification and thus shape the mainstream of Korean history? It seems that this was due to the fact that they had long preserved their unique culture. As is well known, due to its geographical location, Silla was the last among the Three Kingdoms to import advanced culture. Consequently, the establishment of an ancient state system was inevitably delayed. However, this also had the advantage of allowing them to preserve their unique culture for a long time. This tradition of unique culture is thought to have instilled in the people of Silla a strong spirit of independence and self-reliance, and also enabled them to produce excellent leaders. This ultimately led to the unification of the Three Kingdoms.

In the early 10th century, after the fall of Balhae, Goryeo rose to power in its place, and a persistent movement to recover the northern territories began. Goryeo recovered most of Pyongan Province, excluding the Yalu River basin in the northwest, and the Hamgyeong Province region up to Yeongheung in the northeast through the assimilation or conquest of the Balhae people.

Goryeo's northern expansion policy was temporarily halted in the early 13th century with the rise of the Mongol (Yuan) forces. However, it was revived during the mid-14th century transition period between the Yuan and Ming dynasties, leading to the recovery of almost all of Pyongan Province and the Hamgyeong Province region up to Gilju. Goryeo also launched two attacks on the Liaodong region in Manchuria with the aim of expanding into the area.

Our territory expanded to the Yalu River and Tumen River lines in the early 15th century. Sejong the Great inherited the unfinished work of Goryeo, establishing four counties in the upper reaches of the Yalu River to the northwest and opening six fortresses to the northeast, thus securing the borders of that time along the Yalu River and Tumen River lines. Later, there was a period when the four counties were abolished, but this did not signify the abandonment of the territory, so the Yalu River line in the northwest was maintained.


--- (p. 30) ---

In the early 15th century, the borders were established along the Yalu and Tumen Rivers, halting the northern expansion policy. However, since the early 17th century, private migration to Manchuria and the Maritime Province began, with numbers increasing generation by generation, reaching over two million by the 1940s. These migrants were particularly concentrated in the Gando region. Thus, disputes over the sovereignty of Gando arose between the Joseon and Qing dynasties, known as the Gando Problem. In this way, we can rediscover the strength of the Korean people.

### 3. The Development of National History

What stages has Korean society (韓國社會) gone through to reach the present day? Specifically, if we consider the social ruling class (社會的支配勢力) based on the caste system (身分制), how can the flow of Korean history (韓國史) be summarized?

This question should be considered starting from the Paleolithic era (舊石器時代). However, investigations and excavations of the Paleolithic era (舊石器時代) have only recently begun, so we cannot fully understand the social conditions (社會相) of that time. The outline of the social conditions (社會相) begins to emerge from the Neolithic era (新石器時代).

The basic social unit (社會單位) of the Neolithic era (新石器時代) seems to have been the clan (氏族). Within the clan (氏族), there were families (家族), and tribes (部族) composed of several clans (氏族) were also formed. However, the most basic unit (單位) of social organization (社會組織) seems to have been the clan (氏族).

This clan society (氏族社會) lived according to communal principles (共同體的原理). Major clan affairs (氏族會議) were decided in clan meetings (氏族會議), and they are thought to have produced and distributed collectively. Therefore, clan members (氏族構成員) were in an equal relationship (關係) with each other, and even if there was a clan leader (氏族의長), they were merely a representative (代表者) elected by vote (選擧) who could be removed at any time if mistakes were made.

From various characteristics (特徵) of this clan society (氏族社會), we can infer that no privileged class (特權을 갖는身分層) was formed. In other words, all clan members (氏族構成員) were the owners, and they were all the ruling class (支配勢力) that led the clan society (氏族社會).

The formation of a ruling class (支配階層) began in the Bronze Age (靑銅器時代). A clear example of this is the dolmen (支石墓), which was a burial site for an individual.


--- (p. 31) ---

## Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

Some were enormous, with capstones (蓋石) measuring 9 meters in length and weighing 70 tons, transported from dozens of ri away. This suggests that the person buried within, or the one who created it, was a powerful figure (權力者) capable of mobilizing a large number of people.

The newly emerged social (社會的) ruling class (支配勢力) distinguished their residences from those of common farmers (農民). They lived in walled towns (城邑), distinct from villages (村落). These walled towns (城邑) were situated within low hill forts (土城), which were distributed throughout the country.

The new ruling class (支配勢力) residing in these walled towns (城邑) governed the farmers (農民) who lived in villages (村落) and engaged in agriculture (農業). By this time, it is believed that farmers (農民) had already acquired personal land (土地). Consequently, social stratification occurred among the villagers (村落民), with some becoming hired laborers (傭民) or slaves (奴婢). Additionally, villagers (村落民) seem to have cultivated not only their personal land (土地) but also communal land (共有地) belonging to the village (村落). Therefore, it is thought that the village society (村落社會) still maintained a communal (共同體的) character.

These walled-town states (城邑國家) later united to form larger states—confederate kingdoms (聯盟王國). This period is estimated to be around the 4th century BC, coinciding with the introduction of bronze culture (靑銅器文化). However, even after the formation of confederate kingdoms (聯盟王國) and the establishment of kings (國王), the actual ruling class (支配勢力) was likely still the rulers (支配者) of the walled-town states (城邑國家).

With the advent of the Bronze Age (靑銅器時代), a ruling class (支配勢力) emerged, and farmers (農民) began to differentiate into several strata. This was a significant change in the history of social development (社會發展史).

During the Three Kingdoms period (三國時代), society underwent another transformation. The central ruling class (支配勢力) became the nobility (貴族) residing in the capital, who were granted privileges (特權) through a class system (身分制). Central nobility (中央貴族) emerged, taking control of the political (政治), economic (經濟), and cultural (文化) leadership (主導權).

In the case of Goguryeo (高句麗), only the royal family (王族) and the queen's family (王妃族) were eligible for the title of Gochu-ga (古鄒加). In Baekje (百濟), the royal family (王族) and the queen's family (王妃族) monopolized the position of Sangsin (上臣), and high-ranking official posts (長官職) in strategic local areas (地方要地), such as Damna (擔魯), were exclusively held by the royal family (王族). These facts indicate that both kingdoms were ruled by a very narrow circle of noble families (家門) centered around the royal family (王族), forming the social (社會的) ruling class (支配勢力).


--- (p. 32) ---

This aspect is even more evident in the case of Silla (新羅). Silla had eight social classes: the holy bone (聖骨) and true bone (眞骨), along with the six head ranks (頭品) from six head rank (六頭品) to one head rank (一頭品). Among these eight classes, while the holy bone (聖骨) might have been significant, it was the true bone (眞骨) that held the dominant power in politics (政治), economy (經濟), military (軍事), and society (社會) after the period of the unification of the three kingdoms (三國統一期). However, the number of families included in the true bone (眞骨) was extremely limited. Firstly, the royal family, the Kim (金) clan, formed the main lineage, followed by the Park (朴) clan, the family of the queen. Their numbers do not seem to have been very large, and while the Kim Gyeong-shin (金庚信) lineage was also treated as true bone (眞骨), their existence was obscure. Therefore, the core of Silla's ruling class (支配勢力) was the Kim (金) clan among the true bone (眞骨).

However, as Silla entered its later period (下代) at the end of the 8th century, a force challenging the rule of the true bone (眞骨) emerged. One of these was the advancement of the six head rank (六頭品). They possessed scholarly insight and Confucian (儒敎的) education, and were well acquainted with the Tang (唐) examination system (科擧制度), which recruited officials based on individual abilities. Therefore, they criticized the bone rank system (骨品制度) and demanded to be treated equally with the true bone (眞骨).

More significantly, the emergence of clan groups (聚族) occurred. Among these clan groups (聚族), there were those who had moved to the countryside from the true bone (眞骨) or the six head rank (六頭品). However, it seems that many of them were local leaders (村主) who had grown into local powers (土着勢力) from an early period. They acted as city lords (城主) or generals (將官), exercising administrative (行政), military (軍事), and economic (經濟的) dominance over certain regions (地域). This ultimately undermined the power base of the true bone (眞骨) aristocracy (貴族), and peasant rebellions (農民叛亂) that broke out in various places further fueled this. Eventually, these clan groups (聚族) emerged as the real social (社會的) ruling class (支配勢力) in place of the true bone (眞骨).

The fact that King Taejo (太祖) Wang Geon (王建) of Goryeo (高麗) was able to unify the Later Three Kingdoms (後三國) in the early 10th century was also due to the support of these clan groups (聚族). Therefore, he could not avoid pursuing a policy (政策) of alliance (聯合) with the clan groups (聚族). However, as the subsequent kings (王) pursued strong centralization (集權) policies (政策), the clan groups (聚族) gradually lost their independent (獨自的인) power and were either absorbed into the central aristocracy (貴族) or reduced to local officials (鄕吏) in their social (社會的) status (地位). Thus, by the early 11th century (初) (during the reign of King Hyeonjong (顯宗)), Goryeo (高麗) society (社會) transformed into a centralized (集權的) aristocratic (貴族) society (社會).

The newly formed aristocratic (貴族) society (社會) was one that respected social status (身分) based on lineage (血統).


--- (p. 33) ---

Therefore, social advancement was determined not by an individual's (個人) abilities (能力) but by their status (身分). Consequently, marriages (婚姻) were primarily arranged among the nobility (貴族), with the ideal being alliances with powerful families (家門), especially the royal family (王室).

The main power base (勢力) of this aristocratic society (貴族社會) was the capital (開京), modern-day Seoul, and the surrounding regions (近畿地方). Excluding the Kim (金氏) and Choi (崔氏) families of Gyeongju (慶州), their ancestral seats (本貫) were all located south of Jabilryeong Pass (慈悲嶺), west of Daegwallyeong Pass (大關嶺), and north of the Sobaek Mountains (小白山脈).

In the Goryeo (高麗) aristocratic society (貴族社會), civil aristocrats (文臣貴族) held a higher position (優位) than military aristocrats (武臣貴族). The civil and military aristocrat system (文武兩班制度) was introduced early in Goryeo's history, clearly distinguishing families (家門) destined for civil (文臣) or military (武臣) roles. Military aristocrats (武臣) often included soldiers (軍人) who had risen from peasant (農民) backgrounds, and even those of low-born (賤民) origins. While local officials (鄕吏) could become civil aristocrats (文臣) through the civil service examination (科擧), their original status (本來) as local elites (鄕族) did not undermine the dignity (尊嚴性) of civil aristocrats (文臣貴族).

Goryeo's (高麗) status system (身分體制), centered around civil aristocrats (文班貴族), marginalized military aristocrats (武班), creating distinctions (差別) in treatment (處遇). Eventually, military aristocrats (武臣) overthrew the civil aristocrats (文臣貴族), establishing a military regime (武臣政權) by the late 12th century. From this point, military aristocrats (武班) gained equal rights (權利) with civil aristocrats (文班).

While the military aristocrats' (武臣) rebellion (亂) elevated the status (地位) of military officials (武班) to a level formally (形式上) comparable to civil officials (文班), it also greatly unsettled the lower classes (被支配層). Peasants (農民), who formed the base (基底) of society (社會), began movements (運動) to fundamentally (根本的) change the status system (身分體制). Even slaves (奴婢) engaged in powerful emancipation movements (身分解放運動). As a result of these uprisings (民亂), institutions (制度) like hyang (鄕), so (所), and bugok (部曲)—which had persisted since the Silla (新羅) era—gradually (漸次) disappeared (消滅).

Local officials (鄕吏) had a path to enter the civil service (文班) through the civil service examination (科擧), but they were excluded (疎外) from the Iilsi-gye regulation (異日柴科). After the military regime (武臣政權), as farm estates (農莊) expanded (擴大), this exclusion (疎外現象) became more pronounced (突出). Thus, the new officials (新進官僚), often referred to as yangban (士大夫), found themselves in opposition (對立) to the central aristocrats (中央貴族) and powerful families (權門世族). They strongly (強力) desired (希望) a reform (改編) of Goryeo society (高麗社會). Eventually, aligning with the military (武人) forces led by Yi Seong-gye (李成桂) at the end of the 14th century, they succeeded in establishing the Joseon Dynasty (朝鮮王朝), emerging as the new ruling class (支配勢力).


--- (p. 34) ---

When the yangban (士大夫) obtained official positions, they belonged to either the civil (文班) or military (武班) yangban (兩班) class. Thus, the term yangban (兩班) gradually came to refer to the social stratum (身分層) that could hold civil and military yangban positions (兩班職). The generalization of the term yangban occurred during the Joseon Dynasty (朝鮮王朝). Therefore, we can refer to the Joseon era (朝鮮時代), where the yangban stratum (兩班身分層) was the dominant force (支配勢力), as the yangban society (班社會).

The yangban society (兩班社會), which had long enjoyed privileged status (特權的地位), began to collapse after the 17th century, and discrimination based on legitimacy (嫡庶) started to ease. Yangban (兩班) who had been excluded from power (政權) for a long time retreated to the countryside (落鄕), and some even became tenant farmers (小作農), leading to a disintegrative effect (分解作用) on yangban society (兩班社會).

On the other hand, the social advancement (社會的進出) of the middle class (中人) became more pronounced. They broadened their horizons (見聞) and accumulated wealth (財產) through overseas travel (海外旅行), thereby improving their social status (社會的地位). They also began to assert their rightful positions (位置) based on their specialized knowledge (專門的識見) and administrative abilities (行政能力). They showed sensitive reactions to Catholicism (天主敎) and enlightenment ideas (開化思想) and produced many ideological pioneers (思想的先驅者) of the new era.

Among the farmers (農民), some lost their land (土地) and became agricultural laborers (農業勞動者), artisans (手工業), or miners (鑛山勞動者), leading to the emergence of a wage laborer class (賃金勞動者). Meanwhile, with the spread of new transplanting methods (移秧法), large-scale farmers (廣作農) increased, and in cities (都市), merchant magnates (都賈商人) were growing. These large-scale farmers (廣作農) and merchant magnates (都賈商人) were expanding their social influence (社會的影響力) based on their accumulated wealth (財產).

Even the slaves (奴婢) at the bottom of society (社會) were gradually being emancipated (解放). In the case of public slaves (公奴婢), the state (國家) finally abolished the slave registry (奴婢案), freeing them from their lowly status (賤民). This phenomenon began to appear in the case of private slaves (私奴婢) as well. These various phenomena indicate that yangban society (兩班社會) was gradually transforming into a new form of society (社會). In particular, the growth of the enlightenment faction (開化派) in cities (市) and the growth of the Donghak (東學) faction in rural areas (農村) from the late 19th century played a decisive role (決定的役割) in this trend. Thus, the privileges (特權) of the yangban (兩班) were stripped away, yangban society (兩班社會) collapsed, and the old caste system (身分體制) disappeared.

Above, we have examined the development of Korean history (韓國史) centered on the changes in the dominant social forces (社會的支配勢力). The society up to the end of the 9th century, summarized as the bone-rank system (骨品制) of Unified Silla (統一新羅), was one where only the true-bone (眞骨) class


--- (p. 35) ---

## Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

It was a society with a rigid and inflexible caste system (身分制). However, from the early 10th century onwards, it gradually transformed into an aristocratic society based on family ties (門閥貴族社會), broadening the scope of the dominant social forces (支配勢力) and allowing for some degree of mobility between social strata (社會階層). By the late 14th century, it had evolved into a yangban aristocratic society (兩班貴族社會), further accentuating this trend. Finally, by the mid-19th century, the caste system (身分體制) came to an end, marking the beginning of a new era in Korean history (韓國史)—one characterized by modernity (近代的).

### Section 4: Korea's Geopolitical Special Characteristics

#### 1. The Geopolitical Significance of the National Territory

In determining a nation's fate (國家運命決定), geographical conditions (地理的條件) play the most influential role. This is because the quality (質) and quantity (量) of the national territory (國土) and its people (國民) are crucial factors in shaping destiny. Moreover, these factors constitute an unchanging (不變數的) element of security (安保與件).

However, the national territory (國土) cannot be understood solely from a static (靜的) perspective (側面) in relation to security (安保). Dynamic (動的) elements, such as interstate political relations (國家間政治關係), must also be incorporated to grasp the geopolitical (地政學的) reality. For instance, if our national territory (國土) were located next to the state of Chu (楚州), our fate (運命) would have unfolded in a vastly different direction (方向). Similarly, if our surroundings (周邊) were composed solely of weak and small nations (弱少國), our history (歷史) would have taken an entirely different course (內容).

Thus, it is necessary to approach the issue from a geopolitical (地政學的) perspective (側面) that combines static (靜的) geography (地理) with dynamic (動的) political concepts (政治槪念). Central (中央的) and peripheral (周邊的) positions have significantly influenced Korean history (歷史) from a geopolitical (地政學的) standpoint (特性). In this context, we will examine these two positions in relation to security (安保) and explore Korea's (韓國) vulnerabilities (脆弱點) from a lower-dimensional, national defense geographical (國防地理的) perspective (側面). This approach will help us understand some of the unchanging (不變的) challenges (挑戰要因) to our security (安保).


--- (p. 36) ---

## 2. Central Position and Security

The geopolitical characteristics of the Korean Peninsula, which have had a significant impact on our history, can be broadly categorized into two aspects: its central position and its peripheral position.

The central position of the Korean Peninsula includes the following two aspects:
1. Being surrounded by the four major powers of the United States, China, Japan, and the Soviet Union.
2. Being situated between the maritime power of Japan's continental advance and the continental power of China's sphere of influence.

Among these two central position concepts, we will discuss the latter characteristic under the peripheral position section. Here, we will only examine the aspect of the central position within the context of the four-power relationship.

If we consider only the geographical aspect, excluding political elements, Korea is surrounded by the three powers of China, Japan, and the Soviet Union. However, until the Soviet Union's eastward expansion (which was most active from the 1850s to the 1880s) and Japan's modernization following the Meiji Restoration, the concept of a triangular central position could not be established. Instead, the Korean Peninsula was merely considered an appendage to the Chinese continent.

When the Korean Peninsula was in a position subordinate to the Chinese continent, its fate changed in accordance with changes in China (East Asia). The increase in China's influence over Korea and the achievement of unification coincided with the prosperity of the Tang Dynasty. The Mongol invasions of Korea occurred simultaneously with the prosperity of the Yuan Dynasty. The birth of the Joseon Dynasty took place during the transition from the Ming to the Qing Dynasty. The Joseon Dynasty continued to be influenced by China.

However, after the Soviet Union's eastward expansion and Japan's modernization, the influence on the Korean Peninsula was no longer merely a matter of being on the Chinese continent's sphere of influence but involved a tripartite dynamic. The power struggle on the Korean Peninsula in the 1880s can be seen as an example of this. In relative terms, the late Joseon Dynasty was in a central position where its history was determined by the influence of three countries.

After the Russo-Japanese War, Korea came under Japanese rule. Geographically, it was placed in the center of the three powers, but politically, it was subjected to one-sided Japanese influence.


--- (p. 37) ---

## Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

After liberation (解放), the United States (美國) began to exert political influence (政治的影響力) in this region (地域), shifting the central (中央) power dynamics from a tripolar (三强) system to a quadripolar (四强) one. Of course, the quadripolar (四强) relationship (關係) influenced by the United States (美國) after liberation (解放) changed as follows:

1. 1940s: Central (中央的) position (位置) of the U.S. (美) and the Soviet Union (蘇)
2. 1950s: Central (中央的) position (位置) of the U.S. (美), China (中), and the Soviet Union (蘇)
3. 1960s: Central (中央的) position (位置) of the U.S. (美), China (中), the Soviet Union (蘇), and Japan (日)

As seen above, due to the power dynamics (力의 작용) of the quadripolar (四强) political influence (政治的影響力), the central (中央的) position (位置) shifted from a bipolar (二國) to a tripolar (三國) and then a quadripolar (四國) system.

A small country (小國) surrounded by strong nations (强國) tends to fall into the following influences (影響) and fates (運命):

1. Division (分斷) and partition (分割) by great powers (大國)
2. Domination (支配) by one great power (大國) or a group of nations (國家群)
3. Survival (存續) as a buffer (緩衝) or neutral (中立的) zone (地帶)

Among the three, survival (存續) as a buffer (緩衝) or neutral (中立) zone (地帶) is the norm (常例). However, attempts (企圖) to control (掌握) the small country (小國) to maintain a favorable power dynamic (勢力關係) often arise. Before Japan's (日本) domination (支配), it was a buffer zone (緩衝地帶), but after Japan's (日本) victory (勝利) in wars (戰爭) against Qing China (淸國) and Russia (俄), it came under Japan's (日本) unilateral (一方的) domination (支配). After liberation (解放), it fell into the fate (運命) of partition (分割).

In the current state (狀態) of division (分斷) under the quadripolar (四强) central (中央) position (位置), our (我) fate (運命) faces a major (重大) directional (方向) decision (決定) in the following three scenarios (境遇):

One is when the great powers (大國) adopt a policy (政策) of minimal (最小) intervention (介入) (a passive (消極) policy (政策) of withdrawal (손을 떼는)), the concept (槪念) of "decision (決判)" emerges in South and North Korea (南北韓), risking the danger (危險) of war (戰爭). Phenomena (現象) like the withdrawal (撤收) of U.S. troops (美軍) create such conditions (條件).

Another is when the great powers (强大國) pursue (追求) the stabilization (安定) of the status quo (現狀) by turning the region into a buffer zone (緩衝地帶化) (or a neutral zone (中立地帶化)), the danger (危險) of war (戰爭) decreases, but the resolution (解消) of division (分斷), i.e., unification (統一), becomes difficult. The hollowing out (空洞化) or neutralization (無力化) of the collective security (安保) systems (體制) that the U.S. (美國), Communist China (中共), and the Soviet Union (蘇聯) have respectively established with South Korea (韓國) and North Korea (北韓), or their alignment (合致) with the institutionalization (制度化) of peace (平和), or the blessing (保佑) of peace (平和), can be seen as buffering (緩衝化). This implies the freezing (凍結) of the status quo (現狀).


--- (p. 38) ---

Given the central position among great powers, it becomes difficult to achieve unification. In our position, we must consider several paths.
1. We can seek national security through alliances with some great powers. In this case, we can consider alliances with the United States or cooperation with Japan, while North Korea would naturally form alliances with China and the Soviet Union.
2. There could be a way to independently balance and counter the great powers while securing independent security and unification capabilities. This involves simultaneously establishing a self-reliant security posture, maintaining relatively neutral relations among the four great powers, and pursuing a policy direction centered on politics and diplomacy.
3. Another path is to engage in collective security with the backing of great powers while also establishing a self-reliant security posture. This parallel policy direction seems particularly necessary and inevitable for South Korea, even more so than for North Korea.

### 3. Peripheral Position and Security

The Korean Peninsula is currently in a peripheral position in several aspects. These can be exemplified as follows:
1. Geographical Peripheral Zone: Located on the periphery of both the ocean and the continent, South and North Korea are positioned at the forefront of maritime and continental powers, respectively.
2. Political Peripheral Zone: While being at the forefront of the free world and the communist world, South and North Korea are not at the core of global power politics. In terms of power, they still belong to the peripheral zone in global politics.
3. Cultural Peripheral Zone: The Korean Peninsula has not been the origin of globally significant values. Capitalist and communist cultures, rooted in the West and Russia, have penetrated the Korean Peninsula, placing South and North Korea in the cultural periphery rather than the core.
4. Economic Peripheral Zone: Economically, South and North Korea are not part of the core of economic power and have not yet joined the ranks of advanced countries.


--- (p. 39) ---

## Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

can be considered a peripheral region.

As seen earlier, the Korean Peninsula is part of a peripheral region from various aspects, including politics, economy, culture, and geography. However, from a security perspective, its geographical peripheral nature is of utmost importance. Therefore, this section will examine the characteristics of geographical peripherality in more detail. The theory of geographical peripherality with military characteristics originates from both maritime-centric and continental-centric theories. From either perspective, it is clear that the Korean Peninsula is a peripheral region. In other words, the Korean Peninsula belongs to the intermediate peripheral region (Rimland) as described by V.J. Spykman.

First, let's examine the peripherality of the Korean Peninsula from the perspective of maritime-centric theory (A.J. Mahan's argument).

He viewed international politics as a continuous struggle for sea control. His focus was not on land but on the oceans surrounding the land. Oceans serve as excellent transportation routes compared to land, so the country that controls sea routes becomes a world power, according to his argument. Just as Britain's dominance of the oceans led to the collapse of Napoleon's Continental System, historically, significant political and military decisions have been made by countries that control the oceans. In other words, maritime powers have a far superior transportation system and mobility compared to continental powers.

On the other hand, let's examine the peripherality of the Korean Peninsula from a continental-centric perspective.

H. Mackinder is a representative figure of continental-centric theory, and his theory is unique in that it posits the existence of a heartland within the continent. According to his theory, continental power is formed around the heartland, with peripheral regions surrounding it and island (maritime) regions beyond that. According to his theory, the country that controls the heartland region dominates the continent and peripheral regions and ultimately the world.

The heartland of Europe includes Germany, France, and Austria, while the heartland of Asia is China. In this sense, the theory is similar to the Sinocentric worldview. The concept of the Central Plains (中原) in the Sinocentric worldview can be seen as analogous to this. The ruler of the Central Plains governs the peripheral regions.


--- (p. 40) ---

It is because they believed that controlling the periphery (邊部) could lead to controlling the "world" (天下)(세계(世界)).

From the perspective of Sinocentrism (中華思想) or the continental-centric (大陸中心主義的) theory that emphasizes the heartland (心臟大陸), it is clear that the Korean Peninsula (韓半島) is a peripheral (周邊) or marginal (邊部) region (地域), and this is especially true for South Korea (南韓). The peninsula (半島) is contiguous with the Chinese continent (中國大陸), the heartland (心臟地帶) of Asia, and is in contact with the eastern (東方) outlet (出口) of the Soviet Union. Because the Korean Peninsula (韓半島) is located on the periphery (周邊) of the continent (大陸), South Korea (南韓) faces intensified security (安保上) pressures (壓力) from North Korea (北韓), which has the backing of China (中共) and the Soviet Union. Even when it was a unified nation-state (民族國家), it received considerable pressure (壓力) from the immense power of the continent (大陸), but after the division (分斷), South Korea (南韓) has become a "semi-peninsula" (半半島) and thus faces even greater threats (威脅).

Under these geographical (地理的) conditions (與件), our ability to counter the pressure (壓力)(threats (威脅)) from the north must be superior (優位).

As previously discussed, South Korea (韓國) is at the forefront (尖端) of the maritime sphere of influence (海洋勢力圈) and must confront the continental powers (大陸勢力) at their forefront (尖端). Therefore, South Korea (韓國) must pursue a dual (二重) policy (政策): maritime-centric (海洋中心的) cooperation (協力) with maritime nations (海洋國) and a defense policy (防衛政策) to prepare for land (陸上) invasions (侵入). Since this dual (二重) policy (政策) is inherently contradictory (矛盾性), it must be implemented in harmony (調和).

## 4. National Defense Geographical (國防地理的) Characteristics (特徵)

When examining South Korea's (韓國) geography (地理) from the narrower perspective of national defense (國防), several distinctive (特徵的) characteristics (性格) can be identified.

Firstly, it is a peninsula nation (半島國家) that shares land borders (陸地) with China (中共) and the Soviet Union, forming a quadrilateral (四方形) shape.

The Korean Peninsula (韓半島) spans from the 33rd to the 43rd parallel north (北緯), covering a range of 10 degrees, and is located between the 124th and 131st meridian east (東經), resulting in a territorial (國土) configuration (形成) that is shorter east-west (東西) and longer north-south (南北).

Additionally, a peninsula (半島) is formed to the north (北), bordering China (中共) and the Soviet Union.

However, South Korea (南韓) spans from the 33rd to the 38th parallel north (北緯), forming a regular quadrilateral (正四角形) peninsula (半島) shape (狀), resulting in a very narrow territory (國土).

Due to this territorial (國土) formation (形成), we believe that the following influences (影響) are felt from a national defense (國防上) perspective.


--- (p. 41) ---

## Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

① North Korea is in a position to receive immediate support from China and the Soviet Union, whereas we must spend a considerable amount of time receiving support from the United States and Japan, and there are also issues with the deployment of this support. Therefore, Korea faces the difficulty of having to secure support forces locally (stationing).

② The country's small area makes it vulnerable to attacks using modern equipment. Even if North Korean air bases launch modern bombers, South Korean regions could be subjected to air raids within tens of minutes. This is because the air operation depth is short, making it possible to suffer significant damage before countermeasures can be taken. In addition to the short air operation depth, the ground operation depth is also short, meaning that major Korean regions, including the capital area, could be subjected to rocket and long-range artillery attacks from the armistice line.

③ As South Korea is a peninsula, it can receive some defensive help through maritime connections, but it is also vulnerable to infiltration and attacks from the sea, which could cause significant damage. However, since we are bordered by the sea on three sides, unlike North Korea, we have a favorable defensive condition due to the sea. At the same time, having coastal cities (mainly industrial cities) means there is also a risk of significant damage from maritime attacks. The Western Sea has significant tidal differences and many islands, making it difficult to detect enemy spy ships with radar, thus posing a defensive weakness in some aspects.

Secondly, the capital area, including Seoul, is close to the armistice line, placing it within the range of enemy ground artillery attacks.

The targets of military attacks are typically set as military facilities, industrial zones, and cities. However, cities often contain both industrial and military facilities, making major cities prime targets for attacks.

Our capital area includes Seoul and the surrounding cities of Incheon, Bucheon, Anyang, Seongnam, and Uiwang, making it an important region for several reasons.

One reason is that it is one of the important industrial zones. Among South Korea's industrial zones, this


--- (p. 42) ---

The capital region (首都圈) is of great importance. The total production (總生産) generated in the capital region is about twice that of the entire North Korea (北韓). Another aspect is population (人口); the population of the capital region accounts for half of North Korea's (北韓) total population (人口). This exceeds one-fourth of South Korea's (南韓) population (人口). Thus, the capital region (首都圈) holds a central position (位置) for the nation (民族) not only in economic terms (經濟面) but also in political (政治), historical (歷史), and cultural aspects (文化面).

From this perspective, the force (勢力) that controls the capital region (首도권) can be said to lead the nation (民族). This is because the capital region (首都圏) occupies nearly one-third of the nation's (民族) total capacity (力).

However, the capital region (首都圏) is located just 40 km away from the demilitarized zone (休戰線). Therefore, the area where the population (人口) and resources (大) are highly concentrated is a target (地點) for attacks (攻搫) by new long-range (長距離) artillery (砲), and it is also a place where combat aircraft (戰燦機) taking off near the demilitarized zone (休戰線) can reach within minutes (數分).

Thus, North Korea (北韓) will likely be psychologically (心理的) motivated to seize the capital region (首都圈) to lead the nation (民族), and South Korea (韓國) will inevitably have to adopt a concept (槪念) of defending (死守) it. If the capital (首都) of the United States (美國) were within the range (圈) of ground (地上) artillery (砲擊) and a neighboring country (隣接國) had an aggressive (侵略的) inclination towards the United States (美國), what attitude (態勢) would the United States (美國) adopt? We can infer this. This point must be considered the most serious vulnerability (脆弱點) in our national defense (國防) geography (地理).

## 5. Problems (問題點) Arising from Special Characteristics (特殊性)

We have seen how the geopolitical (地政學的) characteristics (特性) of South Korea (韓國) pose security (安保) issues. As a result, we can identify several vulnerabilities (脆弱點):

1. Located in the center (中央) of a great power (强大國), always facing the risk (危険) of invasion (侵攻) by the great power (强大國).
2. Positioned around (周邊) both the ocean (海洋) and the continent (大陸), placed on the line (線上) of potential conflict (衝突).
3. As a peninsula (半島的) and a divided nation (分斷), South Korea (南韓) must endure (感수) disadvantages (不利益) in terms of national defense (國防上).
4. While North Korea (北韓) borders (接境) its supporting forces (支援勢力), South Korea (韓國) is far from its core (核心) supporter (支援國), the United States (美國), putting it at a significant disadvantage (支援上) in terms of support (支援).
5. With its capital region (首都圈) within the range (圈) of ground (地上) artillery (砲擊), South Korea (韓國) must prioritize (優先) security (安保).


--- (p. 43) ---

# Chapter 1 (第1章) Historical Background (史的 背景) of the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動)

Due to the unfavorable geopolitical position (地政學的 位置) we find ourselves in, we must continue to pursue the following policy directions (政策方向):
Strengthening cooperation (協力强化) with maritime powers (海洋勢力) such as the United States (美國), improving or resolving hostile relations (敵對關係解消) with China (中) and the Soviet Union (蘇), efforts to institutionalize peace (平和制度化) to prevent war (戰爭豫防) with North Korea (北傀), and establishing a self-reliant security (自主安保) posture (態勢). The aforementioned directions (方向) may change depending on the historical development (歷史展開) process (過程). Until the early 1960s, security (安保) was pursued with a focus on dependence (依存的) on the United States (美國), but at this stage of history (歷史段階), the focus should be on self-reliant security (自主安保). After a considerable period, we may also need to focus on other policy directions (政策方向).

## Section 5 (第5節) Trials (試鍊) Faced by the Korean People (韓民族)

### 1. National Crisis (國難) Trials (試鍊) and the Korean People (韓民族)

At the time of liberation (解放) in 1945, unlike other newly independent nations (新生國), we had a nation (民族). That nation (民族) was neither unfamiliar (生疎) nor inconvenient (不便) to us. It was, in a word, a historical (歷史的) life form (生命體) with a lineage (由緖) of over 4,000 years. Therefore, for us, 1945 was not merely a year of liberation (解放) from the shackles (桎梏) of Japanese imperialism (日帝), but also a year of regaining (光復) our history (歷史) and making it shine. The meaning of regaining (光復) our history (歷史) and making it shine, given our long history (歷史), is what makes the reality (現實) of today's life (生命) for us, the Korean people (韓民族), not just a short period (時間) of 30 years after liberation (解放), but a deepened (深化) reality (現實) over the 5,000 years since the founding (有史以來) of our country (祖國).

Then, what was the source (根源) of life (生命) that allowed the 30 years after liberation (解放) to be deepened (深化) into the 5,000 years since the founding (有史以來) of Dangun (檀君), the ancestral founder (國祖) of our nation (國)? It was, in a word, the principle (原理) that we had the continuous concept (概念) of a nation (民族) as an eternal subject-life (主體生命).

Here, the concept (概念) of a nation (民族) as a subject (主體) is highlighted as the most precious historical (歷史的) value (價値) before the 50 million of us today.

The nation (民族) that we must once again cherish and reaffirm (가다듬어야 할) before today's history (歷史).


--- (p. 44) ---

The concept of "Jok(族)" as a subject is a name that, in a word, confirms that history(歷史) can never live in our place, and thus it is the most precious ultimate principle of life(生命) that must eternally survive before history(歷史).

The life(生命) of such a precious subject of nationality(民族) that the West today cannot possess even if they make as much noise as they want for just a few hundred years, and even in the leading world(世界) powers of the world history(世界史) such as the U.S.(美) and the Soviet Union(蘇), the concept of this subject of nationality(民族) is not as clear as ours. Here, our national history(民族史) that has been consistently carried on for 4,313 years under the name of the subject of nationality(民族) is bound to be endlessly great and glorious.
