However, the 6-year plan for self-help development by villagers took a balanced development approach, aiming to develop all 33,100 villages across the nation simultaneously. This approach had several inherent issues. Generally, the problems pointed out in developing a backward society include ① lack of capital ② lack of technology ③ low education levels ④ lack of motivation ⑤ religious conservatism, among others. In particular, balanced development in regional community development is never an easy task. Moreover, under conditions where it is difficult to mobilize administrative guidance systematically, it is hard to achieve significant results. Although it is common to adopt the principle of unbalanced development strategy to overcome the difficulties in promoting development projects, the 6-year plan for self-help development by villagers did not deeply consider fundamental solutions to the problems. As a result, the plan failed to be activated and remained merely as a plan, which might have been sidelined.

### 6. National Reconstruction Movement

The National Movement, which began on December 17, 1961 (Law No. 1523, December 16, 1963), was launched after the National Reconstruction Movement (Law No. 622) was abolished and renamed as the National Movement. The National Movement, however, was essentially a continuation of the National Reconstruction Movement. For convenience, this section uses the title "National Reconstruction Movement." The National Movement was defined as "a movement in which all citizens unite under the democratic ideal to build a welfare state, develop their hometowns with the spirit of self-reliance and self-help, and establish a new way of life." To realize this movement ideal, a systematic activity organization was established.


--- (p. 64) ---

It had a central headquarters in the center, with special branches (特別支部) in cities and provinces, and provincial branches (道支部) in provinces. Cities, counties, and districts had city, county, and district branches (市支部, 郡支部, 區支部), each with corresponding committees.

In towns, townships, villages, and neighborhoods, there were town, township, and village committees (邑委員會, 面委員會, 里委員會), which were tasked with overseeing activities related to the national movement (國民運動).

Youth associations (靑年會) and women's associations (婦女會) were established to carry out the national movement (國民運動) under the guidance and supervision of the village and neighborhood committees (里洞委員會).

The main indicators of the activities of the national movement (國民運動) were:
1. Cultivation of national ideology (國民思想涵養)
2. Promotion of fraternity (同胞愛發揮)
3. International cooperation (國際協力)
4. Local development (鄕土開發)
5. Life improvement (生活改善)
6. Vitalization of social atmosphere (社會氣風振作)
7. Local education (鄕土敎育)
8. Guidance and cultivation of youth (靑少年) and women (婦女) (指導育成)
9. Other necessary activities (其他)

To realize the ideological indicators (理念的指標) of the national movement (國民運動), all employees from the director (本部長) down pledged, upon taking office, to "serve as servants of the entire nation (國民全體), being the mother body (母體) of the national union (國民聯合) and the leading body (主導體) of local development (鄕土開發)." With this pledge, they embarked on their journey with vigor.

While the national movement (國民運動) achieved many results across various fields, its essential characteristic (本質的特徵) was its focus on cultural activities (文化活動面). In other words, it lacked a strong emphasis on productive activities (生產活動) directly connected to the economic life (經濟生活) of the residents, making it difficult to deeply root itself in the lives of the people (民衆生活).

Looking at various types of social movements (社會運動) before the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동), the regional community development movement (地域社會開發運動) that took place right after the war lacked an organizational system (體制的) and could not be established even within the administrative organization (行政組織) system. As a result, the Regional Community Development Agency (地域社會開發局) wandered from the Department of Reconstruction (復興部) to the Construction Department (建設部), then to the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (農林部), and finally to the Rural Development Agency (農村振興廳), unable to escape its instability (不安定性).

Furthermore, the 6-year plan for self-help development (自助開發) of village residents (部落民) (1966—1971) initiated by the Rural Development Agency (農村振興廳) lacked vitality (活氣) due to its balanced, comprehensive development approach (全面開發推進).

Another point to note is that the national movement (國民運動) began in 1963, the 6-year plan for self-help development (自助開發) of village residents (部落民) started in 1966, and the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) began in


--- (p. 65) ---

# Chapter 1 (第一章) Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동)

From 1970 onwards, three movements with similar content and characteristics began to coincide with the start of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) in 1970. As a result, it was difficult to avoid general questions about the necessity of continuing movements with similar content, as well as social confusion in perception. Moreover, there were concerns that the integration of various social forces would be difficult to expect. In fact, the "National Movement Organization (國民運動組織)" was dissolved in the mid-1970s, and the "Self-Help Improvement Movement for Village Residents (部落民의 자조개선운동)" was absorbed into the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) through a six-year plan.

From this perspective, when we trace the historical context of social movements in our country, we can understand the prehistory of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) and how the context within that prehistory flows into the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동). In other words, although the naming period of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) is in the 1970s, the blood flowing within the constitution of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) is the same blood that has flowed throughout the history of our nation. Here, we can understand the historical aspects of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동), and the Saemaul Undong (運動) has become a model of a better life movement that compensates for the shortcomings of the movements contained in the prehistory and is a more new and developed form that seeks to realize our desires arising in modern social characteristics.

## Section 7 (第7節) The Launch of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동)

### 1. Departure from Awareness (自覺)

The 1960s can be seen as the preparatory stage for the launch of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동). Efforts were made to free farmers from the shackles of usury that had hindered rural development for thousands of years and to introduce policies to guarantee the prices of agricultural products. In addition, the rural modernization projects of the 1960s can be divided into several categories. First, it established a sense of vocation and national identity among rural residents. Even at that time,


--- (p. 66) ---

About 60% of the total population, who were rural residents, were not settled in their own occupations and thus had not secured their position as citizens. It seems that the idea that national political reform should start with rural reform and a spiritual revolution among rural residents was dominant at that time. Because most citizens, who were rural residents, were not devoted to production, the degree of dependence on foreign countries for food and raw materials increased. As a result, rural areas repeated the vicious cycle of poverty, hindering the economic and social development of our country. Therefore, it was decided to set the goal of self-development and rural development for rural residents as self-defense and national strength enhancement, and this was also one of the top national policies at that time.

Secondly, the foundation for modernizing agriculture was laid and rural administration was innovated. Water resources were developed to attempt all-weather agriculture, land consolidation was carried out to prepare for future agricultural mechanization, and the Rural Development Agency was reorganized to systematize agricultural technology guidance.

Thirdly, rural resource development can be mentioned. Rural resources do not mean only material resources today, but main food crops have become self-sufficient, some raw materials have been replaced by imports, and during the global food crisis in 1973, we were able to endure it to a considerable extent thanks to the agricultural development laid in the 1960s.

Fourthly, there was bold investment in rural areas. To boost the productivity of rural residents and develop rural areas, massive funds have been invested and subsidized since the 1960s to solidify the foundation for development. It is said that about 700,000 rural residents were unemployed in 1962, so the number of potential unemployed would have been even higher.

After the May 16 coup, then Chairman Park Chung-hee of the Supreme Council said in "The Nation, Revolution, and Me," "The rising sun of Korea should not be from the East Sea but from the mountains and fields of the countryside. This is where our hope begins to shine." This shows how closely the countryside in the 1960s was related to the future of the nation. In other words, it was a period when the modernization of the countryside itself did not stop, but the influence it had on the development of the entire nation was immense.

It was at this time that a movement was proposed to develop the countryside and awaken rural residents from the slumber of the old traditional society to participate in the modernization of the motherland. This was the beginning of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement). In other words, the Saemaul Undong was born after about 10 years of gestation.

Another motive for the emergence of the Saemaul Undong was external stimulus. Den


--- (p. 67) ---

# Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

Mark, New Zealand, Israel, Japan, and other countries that have advanced beyond ours generally started their development from rural areas and have become the advanced nations of today. New Zealand has been systematically and plannedly developing agriculture and rural areas since the 1850s, and Israel since the early 1900s. Particularly, New Zealand artificially developed mountains and fields for agriculture, maintaining a per capita national income level of $7,000 since 1972. Meanwhile, countries like the Philippines, Indonesia, and Thailand, which were colonies before World War II, have been rapidly developing since the mid-1950s, which greatly stimulated us.

Although these countries are now far behind ours, around 1970, Thailand had higher income and development projects than ours. Domestically and internationally, we realized that we needed to effectively utilize our human resources to develop our land and refine our technology to develop the resources we possess. Otherwise, our international status would remain dependent on aid or as a weak nation. At that time, the consistent aspiration of our people was how Korea could shed the shackles of being an underdeveloped or backward country, win in the South-North competition, nationalize markets filled with imported goods, and foster self-respect and pride as citizens of an independent nation.

It was at this time that the Saemaul Undong began to ignite in rural areas, and within just 10 years, we reached the level of a middle-power nation. The Saemaul Undong achieved today's results through the blood, sweat, and tears of the entire nation. For example, in 1971, the Saemaul projects amounted to 12.2 billion won, of which 4.1 billion won was government support. The rural people achieved more than three times the support amount. In 1972, out of the total achievement of 31.3 billion won, the residents' effort and investment amounted to 21.1 billion won, accounting for 67% of the total achievement.

In 1962, the per household farm income was 62,000 won, but by 1979, it exceeded 2 million won. In 1960, the per capita national income was $81. Although we cannot compare the prices and currency values of that time one by one, it is undeniable that we were at the level of a backward country in terms of social and economic standards. With this situation, we felt insecure in the competition with North Korea, which was the dominant view at that time.


--- (p. 68) ---

North Korea had been implementing the Chollima Movement since the 1950s and later shifted to the Three Revolutionary Movements, focusing on party-led production. While this approach unified the national spirit and promoted development projects, by the 1960s, North Korea's per capita income had surpassed ours.

During this period, South Korea experienced a strong urban-oriented trend in rural areas, while cities were filled with selfishness and decadence. The social and economic gaps between urban and rural areas were widening. In essence, we were in a perilous state where social values were lacking.

Starting in 1962, while executing the Five-Year Economic Development Plan, we somewhat addressed these weaknesses. However, we lacked a clear goal to establish a sense of agency. It was at this juncture that the Saemaul Undong, targeting rural revitalization, was proposed. Reflecting on this period, the initiation of the Saemaul Undong was indeed a fortunate turn of events.

## 2. Practical Implementation of Resolutions Aimed at Modernization

On April 22, 1970, the government convened a nationwide meeting of local governors to discuss measures to promote self-help efforts in rural areas, with cooperation among farmers, relevant agencies, and assigned personnel as a prerequisite. Then, on May 6 of the same year, a resolution was passed to conserve the national territory by emphasizing the importance of the Saemaul Undong. This marked the official beginning of the Saemaul Undong.

The Saemaul Undong was initiated in rural areas for several reasons. Firstly, as previously mentioned, agriculture, which was the livelihood of the majority of the population, played a significant role in the national economy and was a key industry at the time.

Internally, rural areas needed to re-establish values to serve as a spiritual pillar for rural residents. Additionally, it was essential to mobilize the latent human resources in rural areas for social and economic production, transforming idle labor into productive force. In other words, the movement aimed to spark a spiritual revolution among rural residents, scattered due to individual small-scale management, and to innovate their traditional and stagnant social lives through cooperation. Using this as a foundation, the movement sought to modernize the production process by investing some capital and technology, while simultaneously improving living conditions and production facilities.


--- (p. 69) ---

# Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) aimed to induce rural development (農村開發) led by the citizens (國民).

At the beginning of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), there was much discussion about the purity (純粹性) of its purpose (目的) and the conditions (條件) for its success (成敗). Given the circumstances (條件) at the time, there were doubts (疑懼心) about whether it could develop into a revolutionary (革新的) rural development (農村開發) movement (運動), and concerns (念慮) that it could be politically (政治的) exploited (利用). Although there were some trial and error (施行錯誤) in the process, these concerns did not significantly hinder the progress of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement).

The inaugural (出帆) project (事業) of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) was an environmental improvement (環境整備事業) initiative in rural areas (農村). The government (政府) provided 335 units of cement to each village (里洞), and residents (住民) utilized the idle labor force (遊休勞動力) during the farming off-season (農閑期) to improve their living environment (住居環境) through the Saemaul beautification (新村美化) project (事業).

The goal (目標) of the Saemaul beautification (新村美化) project (事業) was to test (試驗) the spiritual (精神的) cooperation (協同) of the residents (住民) and improve (整備) their living environment (住居環境).

This experimental (試驗) project (事業) yielded remarkable results (成果). In 1971, a total of 7.2 million people (延人員) participated in the project (事業). The residents (住民) themselves were the most surprised by the outcomes (成果) of this experimental (試驗) project (事業). They derived (導出) the principle (原理) that cooperation (協同) leads to self-reliance (自立). The fact that Indonesia's regional (地域) development (開發) projects (事業) also provide a certain amount of funding (金額) to villages (單位) to encourage self-driven (自助) development (開發) suggests that the principles (原理) of our Saemaul (新村) projects (事業) are highly regarded (評價).

Similar to our country, New Zealand, which has developed (開發) its mountainous (山岳) terrain (國土) into one of the world's leading (有數) agricultural nations (農業國), is said to have achieved this through the pioneering (開拓的) efforts (努力) of its residents (住民).

In July 1971, an analysis (分析) of the project's (事業) achievements (成果) up to that point led to the establishment of a new direction (方向) for the movement (運動). It was found that villages (單位) with capable (有能) and dedicated (獻身的) leaders (指導者), as well as strong (旺盛) community (協同) and development (開發) awareness (意識) among residents (住民), achieved greater (成果) results (成果) in the experimental (試驗) project (事業). From this, the principles (原理) of the Saemaul Undong (新村運動) were established as diligence (勤勉), self-help (自助), and cooperation (協同). The movement (運動) began to emphasize (力點) spiritual (精神的) unity (團結) and cooperation (協同) among residents (住民) over material (物質的) growth (成長). The driving force (推進) of the project (事業) lies in the residents (住民) with strong (旺盛) development (開發) aspirations (意慾), who unite (團結) around their leaders (指導者) as a focal point (求心點) to achieve (達成) the project's (事業) goals (成果).

After the experimental (試驗) phase (段階), the direction (方向) of the Saemaul Undong (新村運動) was established (定立) and systematized (體系化) in 1972.


--- (p. 70) ---

It was a matter of the year. Even critics acknowledged it as the most wholesome national movement, and researchers and writers began to handle rural development in their own ways. Theoretically, the development process of the Saemaul Undong was set to improve the rural environment and promote spiritual development, leading to increased income. The direction of the Saemaul Undong was also expanded from a rural development movement to a national movement that all citizens should practice. Initially, the government led the Saemaul Undong, which was criticized as being government-led and thus incorrect. During the experimental period, local government agencies were involved in planning, technology, and financial support, but over time, efforts were made to shift to civilian-led initiatives, excluding support. From the beginning, village development committees organized in each village oversaw the promotion of projects, and in some villages, these organizations handled everything from planning to promotion.

The most difficult task in the early stages of the movement was planning the projects, the residents' project execution skills, and the leader problem. Leaders needed to be trustworthy and have strong leadership, but even if they had the qualifications, they had to endure immense self-sacrifice. Projects that surpassed planning and technology had to match the residents' interests and abilities. Even if the planning was well done, if the technical training of the project executors was insufficient, it could lead to losses and not greatly benefit the residents' welfare, as development theory is related to training. We repeated such experiences in the early stages. That is why we established the Saemaul Leader Training Institute to cultivate leaders and educate numerous residents through various levels of technical training. Now, if a village has capable leaders, simply providing motivation, necessary materials, or financial support can equip the village with the ability to execute both village and regional projects.

However, we need to cultivate more successors for the leaders overseeing the projects. The current leaders were in their 30s or 40s at the inception. We need to train successors to replace them and provide profit motives to encourage them to stay in the rural areas. According to a 1979 survey, some villages had no members or only a few members in their village youth clubs or Saemaul youth clubs. By the 1990s, when the rural population was about 20% of the total population, even more capable leaders would be needed.


--- (p. 71) ---

### Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

Our Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) began to be actively promoted in rural areas and encouraged participation from urban residents and social leaders starting in 1973. From this point, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) was referred to as a nationwide action philosophy, a movement to lay the groundwork for unification, or a great national revitalization movement. In terms of economic development, it was pursued as a movement to transform the entire country into a workplace, to produce all labor, and to turn all citizens into technicians. The guiding principles of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) at this time were as follows: First, it should be developed as a voluntary national movement in which both rural and urban residents participate. Second, as an income-increasing movement, it should create a permanent foundation suited to the abilities of the residents and the characteristics of the region. Third, it should be developed and implemented as an organized practical movement with no trial and error. Fourth, the system for promoting policies should be strengthened. Each agency unified the business entities they had been operating separately to some extent.

Thus, starting in 1973, a comprehensive and systematic direction for the movement was established for the first time. The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) set at this time was, in one word, a movement for the modernization of the fatherland. Ten years prior, modernization was an urgent proposition under the same circumstances as ours, and clear goals had to be set. The goals were spiritual development of the residents, establishment of social order and environmental improvement for social development, economic development for improving the standard of living, and modernization of customary lifestyles for life improvement.

First, the purpose of national spiritual development was to induce self-awareness that the organization is superior to the individual by making cooperation the main axis and changing the idea to a collective one, as the unique subjectivity had been difficult to discern due to the long dominance of Confucian (儒) ideology, poverty-induced resignation, and the coexistence of Western materialism and individualism. The aim was to establish a new worldview, professional view, and national view, and to create a new culture. In other words, it was to reclaim our traditional spiritual culture, which was being overshadowed by foreign cultures, and to construct a new spiritual culture, and to make us aware of the spiritual attitude we should have in an international situation. This was the spiritual development movement.

Sun Yat-sen (孫文) said at the beginning of the 20th century (世紀) when Western culture (西歐文化) swept through China (中國), "A nation (民族) that knows how to keep its culture (文化) alive will not perish even if the state (國家) does."


--- (p. 72) ---

We said that we would not perish (滅亡) and that we would eventually revive. I think it is undeniable that our consciousness of being the main actors (主體) was once similar to that of early 20th-century China.

With the launch of the Saemaul Undong (運動), I believe we also came to possess a historical consciousness (歷史意識) of living in an era (時代) where we have personal (個人) views on life (人生觀) and national (國民) perspectives on the country (國家觀). The establishment of such value systems (價値觀) implies the establishment of ideologies centered around the main actors (主體思想), and the main actors (主體性) must actively and voluntarily act (作用) as the main actors (主體), regardless of whether they are individuals (個人) or a nation (民族). To establish a consciousness of being the main actors (主體意識), we must clearly distinguish what is ours and what tasks we face, and develop and preserve our unique (固有) conditions (條件) and environment (環境) in a creative and active (能動的) manner.

Secondly, to live a convenient and efficient cultural life (文化生活), we must organize and develop our living environment (生活周邊). The first tangible business (有形事業) undertaken at the beginning of the Saemaul Undong (運動) was environmental improvement (環境改善) because of this. Environmental improvement (環境改善) can also be a preliminary stage (前段階) for economic development (經濟開發). Roads (道路), ports (港灣), electricity (電氣), and telecommunications (通信) are conditions (條件) for economic development (經濟開發), just as housing (住宅), farm roads (農路), medical facilities (醫療施設), improvement (改良), and mechanization of farming (營農機械化) are for rural development (農村開發). At the beginning of the Saemaul Undong (運動), rural electrification (電化) was less than half of all farms (農家), but now it is close to 100%. Along with the Saemaul Undong (運動), the spread of agricultural machinery (農機械) and the expansion of medical and health facilities (醫療保健施設) began. The reason for rural exodus (離農) in the 1960s (年代) was due to differences in living (生活), education (敎育), and culture (文化).

The second business (事業) for improving living culture (生活文化) was the scientification (科學化) of living means (生活手段) and the improvement (改善) of living attitudes (生活態度). Therefore, with the launch of the Saemaul Undong (運動), we began to improve water and sewage systems (上下水道), modernize fuel (燃料), and improve housing (住宅). In 1969 (年), we aimed to change the traditional Confucian ritual formalism (儒學形式主義儀禮) into practical rationalism (實質合理主義) according to the family ritual regulations (家庭儀禮準則), save time (時間), curb consumption expenditure (消費支出), and create a productive and healthy environment (生產健全風土). Initially, there were some side effects (副作用) from this. For example, it was difficult to spread alcohol (飮酒) during the busy farming season (農繁期), and there were no nostalgic activities (鄕愁活動) to enjoy during holidays (名節) or the farming off-season (農閑期), which led to the elimination of recreational activities (娛樂) that regenerate productive emotions (生產感情) and the extinction of local arts (地方藝術).

There were also instances of waste (浪費) of materials (资材) and labor (勞動力) due to technical immaturity (技術未熟) when building new fences (新築), bridges (橋梁), and public bathhouses (共同沐浴湯). Additionally, there was the stubbornness (固執) of village elders (元老) who insisted that ancestral rites (祭饌) could not be performed with methane gas (메탄가스), all of which occurred at the beginning (始作).


--- (p. 73) ---

# Chapter 1: Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

The third aspect is the development projects in the economic sector. When the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) was launched, it was expressed as the "Well-Living Movement (運動)," which meant liberation from poverty. Now, ten years later, it can be asserted that the poverty of the past no longer exists in rural areas. At that time, the Second Five-Year Economic Development Plan was underway, and the Saemaul income augmentation projects were implemented in accordance with both annual plans and village characteristics.

To increase the income of residents, the government took charge of land consolidation, agricultural machinery supply, new variety promotion, and technical education, while residents transformed traditional agriculture into modern agriculture through compost production, soil improvement, and the introduction of favorable cropping systems. The achievement of self-sufficiency in rice for the first time in 1976 can also be attributed to the success of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement). Since the early days of the rural Saemaul projects, food production augmentation has been a core component, which also served as the center of farm household income augmentation.

For this reason, during the abnormal weather conditions of 1972, there were instances of distrust in new varieties, and there are still some shortcomings in the improvement of crop cultivation techniques. The high rate of feed imports is also due to this. Efforts must be made to improve management, support prices, and enhance crop production.

The modernization of the distribution structure was also one of the early Saemaul projects. Through the joint shipment of products and the joint purchase of daily necessities, time and labor were saved, and economic benefits were secured. Even today, the village purchasing and selling market, primarily operated by women's associations, is one of the successful examples from the early days.

Since its launch, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) has faced the ongoing challenge of overcoming rural economic issues without resolving them satisfactorily. Unlike the kibbutzim of Israel, it operates as independent family farms due to the family system and the independent management of small farms. Efforts have been made to find methods that do not disrupt this structure while achieving large-scale management effects, but so far, only partial cooperation through the sharing of labor and the joint use of agricultural equipment has been possible. Such cooperation has been a part of rural society, so significant progress is unlikely.

### 3. Expansion of the National Vanguard

The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), which began in rural areas, spread to cities, factories, workplaces, schools, and households from the mid-1970s and is now influencing many developing countries around the world.


--- (p. 74) ---

# Rural and Urban Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

The Rural Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) is considered to have been completely successful, but other Saemaul Undong movements require further research and development.

Cities, unlike rural areas, are open societies composed of heterogeneous groups, making it difficult to set common goals for businesses. Additionally, the profit motives of different entities vary, which also poses a challenge. However, the Saemaul Credit Cooperatives, organized by neighborhood (dong), workplace, and school units, are the most prominent success stories of urban Saemaul Undong.

The first places to adopt the Saemaul Undong in cities were factories, where the members share the same profit motive, forming a homogeneous group. The Saemaul Undong in factories primarily aims to improve labor-management cooperation, work efficiency, and productivity to reduce costs. Part of the resulting profits is returned to the workers, further promoting the movement. Additionally, the Saemaul Undong in factories strengthens bonds among employees, fosters pride in their industrial work, and improves the factory environment. Some factories have even established affiliated schools to provide regular education for their employees, something unheard of before the Saemaul Undong.

In the early days of the Saemaul Undong, the rural population was large, and the proportion of industry was low. However, the manufacturing sector has since grown, and exports now drive the national economy. The creative efforts of factory workers significantly impact the economy, and given the large population in the manufacturing sector, their Saemaul Undong initiatives extend to urban society and families. Although it has only been a decade since its launch, the social and economic resources developed through the Saemaul Undong are immeasurable. It is no exaggeration to say that we have acquired the ability to cope with the resource wars of today through the Saemaul Undong. Reflecting on it now, the Saemaul Undong was well begun, and it should be sustained perpetually without any bystanders to solidify the foundation for national prosperity.


--- (p. 75) ---

## Chapter 2 (第2章) The Fundamental Spirit of the Saemaul Undong (運動)

### Section 1 (第1節) The Guiding Ideology of the Saemaul Undong (運動)

#### 1. The Will for National Modernization (祖國近代化)

The two major tasks of national revival (民族中興)—national unity (民族統合) and national development (民族發展)—are essentially issues of national modernization (祖國近代化). Generally, modernization (近代化) has become a common challenge for newly independent countries, including Korea (韓國), to address in the latter half of the 20th century (世紀). All are grappling with the overarching theme (大命題) of modernization (近代化), striving to achieve their goals (目標) more swiftly and efficiently. However, there are significant differences in the situational conditions (狀況的) of modernization (近代化) that each country faces, as well as in the capacity (能力) of their political systems (政治體制) to adjust (調整) and absorb (吸收) these changes.

These differences manifest in the conceptualization (槪念) of modernization (近代化)—what (무엇을) to target (設定) and how (어떻게) to approach it—and the processes (過程) through which modernization (近代化) should be achieved. In other words, there are differing views on what (무엇을), how (어떻게), and through what processes (過程) modernization (近代化) should be accomplished. These questions are often collectively referred to as the "model (模型) of modernization (近代化)." What model (模型) is suitable for modernizing (近代化) a newly independent country (新生國)? These queries are directly linked to the will (意志) for national modernization (祖國近代化) that the Saemaul Undong (運動) aspires to embody.

##### A. The Content of Modernization (近代化)

The issue of modernization (近代化) or the development (發展) of newly independent countries (新生國) began to attract significant attention from social scientists (社會科學者) in the 1950s (年代). Initially, modernization (近代化) was equated with the problem (問題) of economic development (經濟發展). However, this perspective gradually evolved, recognizing that economic development (經濟發展) was just one aspect of the broader concept (槪念) of modernization (近代化).


--- (p. 76) ---

It has become evident that economic (經濟的) factors alone cannot achieve this. As a result, while modernization (近代化) had previously focused on economic development (經濟發展), attention has now turned to both economic (經濟的) and non-economic (經濟外的) factors. Consequently, social development (社會發展) and political development (政治發展) have become prerequisites or parallel conditions for economic development (經濟發展). This shift has led to the term "modernization (近代化)" encompassing all aspects, including economics (經濟), society (社會), politics (政治), and culture (文化). In other words, the answer to "what to modernize (近代化)" is the development of a specific society's or nation's political (政治), economic (經濟), social (社會), and cultural (文化) domains.

In our context, recognizing this meaning of modernization (近代化), political development (政治發展) involves localizing democracy (民主主義), economic (經濟) and social development (社會發展) entail building a welfare state (福祉國家) through industrialization (產業化), and cultural development (文化發展) aims to overcome national division (民族分斷) and achieve the flourishing of a national culture (民族文化) based on 5,000 years of history (歷史) and tradition (傳統).

## B. Exploring Methods of Modernization (近代化)
When defining modernization (近代化) in this way, the question arises: "How can modernization (近代化) be achieved?" Various perspectives on methods (方法) need to be examined.

Firstly, there is the general theoretical (一般理論) issue in the modernization (近代化) of developing countries (後進國): how to connect with the past (過去) tradition (傳統). In other words, should modernization (近代화) be pursued in a state of disconnection from the past (過去), as in the case of France's modernization (近代化), or should it be pursued in continuity with the past (過去)? This is the choice between disconnection (斷絶) and continuity (連續). This discussion has long been raised by Western scholars (西洋學者) as a methodological model (方法모델) for pursuing modernization (近代化). Depending on the scholar (學者), their stance (立場) varies. Some argue that modernization (近代化) must necessarily occur in a state of disconnection from the past (過去), claiming that traditional societies (傳統社會) inherently contain elements (要素) that hinder modernization (近代化). They assert that without removing these elements (要素), it would take a long time (時間) to pursue modernization (近代化). This argument has the advantage of potentially shortening the time (時間) required for modernization (近代化). In other words, modernization (近代化) is, to some extent, a competition among already advanced nations (國家) in the global (世界) context and also a competition among newly born nations (新生國). Therefore, for us, shortening the time (時間) is crucial.


--- (p. 77) ---

## Chapter 2: The Fundamental Spirit of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

The method of modernization (近代化) must be carefully chosen. Today, the relationship between advanced nations (先進國) and newly emerging countries (新生國) is often compared to the fable of the industrious hare and the tortoise, illustrating the satire of the "eternal laggard" (永遠한 後進) who can never catch up with the advanced hare (先進). This highlights the difficulty of shortening the time (時間) required for modernization (近代化).

In our current journey towards modernization (近代化), the influence of past (過去) customs (폐습) is significant. The overly authoritarian (權威主義的) so-called yangban culture (兩班文化) is one example. While most of these customs have been corrected (是正) through the universalization (普遍化) of a rationalistic (合理主義的) spirit (精神) via the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), remnants such as family ties, clan affiliations, and regionalism still pose obstacles to modernization (近代化). Although removing these traditional (傳統) cultural (文化) vices (惡習) does not necessarily mean a complete break (斷絶) from the past (過去), our methods (方法) and principles (原理) for advancing modernization (近代化) must continue to evolve (發展).

On the other hand, there are drawbacks to choosing modernization (近代化) through a complete break (斷絶) from the past (過去). While such a break may offer the advantage (長點) of shortening time (時間), abruptly eliminating pre-modern (前近代的) traditions (傳統) can lead to severe social (社會) chaos (混亂). The mass migration (移住) of rural populations (農村人口) to cities (都市) due to early industrialization (工業化) has become a headache for countries advancing industrialization (產業化). Considering this, a sudden break (斷絶) from the past (過去) risks destroying the entire society's (社會全體) consensus (共感帶). This drawback is particularly noteworthy in our case, given that our homeland (祖國) is divided (分斷). We cannot ignore their intentions to ensnare the entire Korean Peninsula (韓國社會) in the chaos (混沌) of communism (共產主義) while we merely pursue the fruit of time (時間) shortening (短縮).

Thus, it is difficult to simply choose one approach when considering how to handle past (過去) issues (問題) in the pursuit of modernization (近代化). Given our situation, we cannot afford to remain idle and accept the label of eternal "laggard" (後進). We must create our own methods (方法). If we are to reap the benefits (長點) of time (時間) shortening (短縮) while preventing the sudden social (社會) chaos (混亂) caused by a break (斷絶), we must overcome these challenges through a uniquely Korean (韓國的) and innovative (獨創的) approach to modernization (近代化). This logical (論理的) conclusion, when viewed in light of our society's (社會) efforts towards modernization (近代化), indicates that the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) has been actively promoted since the 1970s (年代).


--- (p. 78) ---

The village movement (運動) is, in fact, a creative (獨創的) method (方法) of modernization (近代化) that overcomes such contradictions (矛盾).

Another perspective (視燈) on the method (方法) of modernization (近代化) is the strategic (戰略) choice (選擇) between modernizing (近代化) the environment (環境) or modernizing (近代化) humanity (人間). Modernization (近代化) is, after all, about living well. And living well means striving for a democratic welfare society (民主福社社會), where all citizens (國民) enjoy freedom (自由) and equality (平等) in a prosperous environment (環境). However, in pursuing (達成) this goal (目標), a strategic (戰略) choice (選擇) is necessary (必要): should humanity (人間) or the environment (環境) be modernized (近代化) first (先)? This dilemma (問題狀況) is often expressed (表現) as the question, "Should the clothes fit the body, or should the body fit the clothes?" or as the debate over whether democratization (民主化) or industrialization (產業化) should come first (先行). This is a well-known (周知) fact (事實).

In reality (現實), this issue (問題) has been a core (核心) task (課題) for Korean politics (韓國政治) over the past 30 years. Since the founding (建國) of our nation, we have advocated (標榜) an open society (開放社會). However, the rapid development (發達) of modern mass communication (現代 메스콤) has transmitted (傳達) Western modern trends (現代思潮) without time difference (別時差), leading to a rapid Westernization (西歐化) of our "mind" (머리). Meanwhile, the challenges (逆境) of industrialization (產業化) have left us without the "physical strength" (體力) to support these incoming modern trends (現代的 思潮), resulting in an imbalance (不均衡) between mind and body (身體). In reality (現實), poverty (가난) envelops our environment (環境), yet our minds (머리) strive to emulate (닮아가려 함) the thoughts (생각) of citizens (國民) from advanced nations (先進國家), leading to entirely misplaced (엉뚱한) social (社會) deviant behavior (逸脫行爲). Examples (一例) of this include the hippie culture (히피문화) and the inappropriate (격에 맞지 않는) leisure (레저) craze (선풍). Simultaneously (同時), young university (大學) students (층) have mistakenly (착각) believed (착각) that Western freedom (西歐의 자유) is our freedom (우리의 자유), advocating (內掛) slogans (口號) like "democratization (民主化)" and exacerbating (加重) social (社會) chaos (混亂). Regardless (別個) of whether they truly (本質的) understood (알고) the meaning (意味) of democracy (民主主義) and acted (行動) accordingly (한 것인가는), it is clear (분명) that they never had (全然) the opportunity (機會) to properly (제대로) digest (소화) and grasp (攄得) its meaning (意味). To this extent (만큼), Korean democracy (韓國的 민주主義) has yet to take root (뿌리를 내리지 못한 상태).

The question of whether to fit the clothes to the body (옷을 몸에 맞추느냐) or the body to the clothes (몸을 옷에 맞추느냐) cannot exist (前提) without a prior (前提) recognition (認識) of the Korean (韓國的) "territory" (터) that aspires (指向) to modernization (近代化). The modernization (近代化) of a newly born nation (新生國) is often likened (比喩) to a race (競走) where two athletes (두 선수) run (달리는) with a triangular belt (삼각끈) tied (매고) to their ankles (발목).


--- (p. 79) ---

## Chapter 2: The Fundamental Spirit of Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

If the way you think differs, you will fall if the speed at which you lift your feet is different. This is the same principle as causing social conflict and friction during the process of modernization. On the other hand, if the thoughts of two athletes are in agreement, they can reach the goal smoothly and quickly.

The problem of the method of modernization can only be overcome when the perception of the "field" is premised. The answer to the question of "how" to modernize can be answered as "in a way that suits the Korean situation." This means that industrialization and democratization should be promoted on the coordinates of Korean industrialization and the coordinates of Korean democracy, and ultimately, a Korean democratic welfare society should be realized. Such a problem of choosing the method of modernization should become one of the guiding principles that the Saemaul Undong should pursue.

### Da. Development of Modernization Promotion Elements

In promoting modernization, there is also the issue of whether to prioritize endogenous elements or focus on exogenous factors such as science and technology. In the development of modern societies, especially in the case of Western Europe, it is a well-known fact that science and technology were the central driving forces of modernization. Science and technology played a central role in industrialization and modern nations were formed in Western societies based on them. In order to achieve the goal of industrialization in modernization, it is impossible to skip the stage of industrialization, which is essential for achieving this goal, without advanced science and technology. In this sense, the influence of exogenous elements on our modernization process is immense. However, the problem is that science and technology are not free or given away for free. At least for the advanced countries that possess them, it is the only means to enjoy their current advanced status forever. Therefore, the exogenous elements essential for our modernization are inevitably transmitted to developing countries with the ideology of advanced countries colored. From this perspective, science and technology can be seen as another nationalist element. This is why terms like American nationalism and European nationalism are often used today. Therefore, when industrialization and modernization are carried out through exogenous elements, it is easy to achieve the goal by utilizing the accumulated science and technology of advanced countries, but


--- (p. 80) ---

Accepting the permanent dominance of foreign culture means that we must also accept the premise of being a permanently underdeveloped country.

On the other hand, if we choose an indigenous approach, we have the advantage of being able to establish our own unique culture and traditions, but it requires a long time and national sacrifice. Nevertheless, in modernization, what is truly important is the indigenous approach. In other words, while the seed may come from outside, the sprout must grow from the soil of our own country. Therefore, in modernization, indigenous factors must be the main axis.

It is a fact that exogenous factors are also important elements of modernization. However, without the soil of indigenous, traditional culture, industrialization and modernization are meaningless. The subject of the modernization we aspire to is based on the nation as the basic unit, and there is a proposition that the roots of the nation's cultural soil must be planted. In this sense, modernization is referred to as "modernization of the fatherland" and "revival of the nation."

The answer to whether we should prioritize exogenous or indigenous methods in modernization can be replaced by the answer that our goal is the modernization of the fatherland and the revival of the nation. And the pressure exerted by exogenous factors should be resolved through our autonomous strength, establishing an equal or cooperative relationship with advanced countries.

### La. Stages and Consciousness Revolution of Modernization

When we grasp the issue of modernization in terms of concepts, methods, and processes, it ultimately comes down to the question of what stages, or processes, we go through to achieve our goals. This is often referred to as the stages or process model of modernization. Accurate recognition of the stages of modernization in our fatherland is important in that it provides a guiding direction for promoting the Saemaul Undong as part of the modernization movement.

Even among scholars in advanced countries dealing with modernization issues, there is recently a growing skepticism about the old claim that modernization follows a single direction with a certain set of stages or processes. This trend acknowledges that there are various paths to modernization. Nevertheless, it is important to consider which path leads to modernization. This is similar to the need for a design plan before construction.


--- (p. 81) ---

## Chapter 2: The Fundamental Spirit of Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

This is for the same reason.

It is commonly known that the stages of modernization are often divided into four or five stages, which is considered a general classification method for the modernization of developing countries. The common characteristics of such general theories are that the process of modernization must first achieve the formation of a nation-state. After this stage, the process enters the stage of achieving industrialization, and when industrialization is completed, the final goal is to develop towards prosperity or a welfare society. A.F.K. Organski, an authority in the study of modernization models for developing countries, emphasizes that this process of modernization is a path that all advanced countries have consistently followed, and that they had to endure arduous struggles and extremely difficult journeys along the way.

From this perspective, it is easy to infer that the process of modernization of our homeland will inevitably be a difficult path. First, the goal of forming a nation-state, which is indicated as the first stage of modernization, remains an unresolved task for us. This situation gives rise to the greatest national goal of security and peaceful unification, and thus leads to the proposition that the path to the modernization of our homeland must be connected to unification. The arduous struggle for unification is a process of modernization that we must necessarily achieve, and it should also be an ideology directly linked to the goals of industrialization and the realization of a welfare society, which are the ultimate goals of modernization.

At least, if we condense the path to modernization in terms of the process, we are in a situation where all stages of modernization overlap. From the perspective of national desire for modernization, this reality presents the task of almost simultaneously resolving the demands for unification, industrialization, and welfare, which are the goals of the various stages of modernization. Therefore, the path to modernization for us is more arduous and difficult than for any other country, and strong will and patience become absolute prerequisites to overcome it.

In our situation, where we must simultaneously pursue the overcoming of division, industrialization, democratization, and the realization of a welfare society, the path of modernization may simultaneously face both progress and crisis. Therefore, the direction of the modernization of our homeland must be able to withstand this.


--- (p. 82) ---

A comprehensive strategy must be developed. The common denominator of such a strategy is its consciousness-based nature. Therefore, the only alternative to overcoming the crisis is to absorb and integrate the Korean situation in a development-oriented manner through a revolution in consciousness.

As a basis for modernization, consciousness must be integrated as a whole while being diverse in content. In other words, to prevent individual consciousnesses from conflicting and creating dissonance, they must be sublimated into a unified ideology. This integrated ideology may manifest as a movement or an ideology, but it must essentially embody a revolution of the spirit.

The reason why our advocated national modernization must be driven as a whole by a spiritual revolution is that only the result of consciousness can generate a creative force capable of overcoming problems that arise in the methods and processes of promoting modernization.

For modernization to be pursued, an integrated spirit is necessary. This can be explained by analogy to the law of contradiction in an old Chinese story. Contradiction, meaning "spear" and "shield," implies that their relationship can cause friction and conflict, much like the repeated demands of modernization. In other words, an all-powerful spear and an all-powerful shield, by their very nature of conflicting, cannot maintain their initial power and must lose their meaning. For example, in the methods of modernization, the argument that industrialization is a shortcut to modernization and the claim that democratization is a shortcut to modernization are tasks that must be resolved simultaneously for us, yet they cannot be resolved simultaneously. The method to overcome this contradiction is to maintain the power of an all-powerful spear and an all-powerful shield without causing them to conflict. In other words, instead of two owners sharing the spear and shield, if one person simultaneously possesses both, a situation where the spear must be blocked by the shield or the shield must be pierced by the spear will never occur.

The theory of spiritual revolution in modernization is the same. Industrialization and democratization are

## Chapter 2: The Fundamental Spirit of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

Rather than dividing among multiple owners (主人) and creating opposition (對立), the Saemaul Undong aims to absorb all these elements into a single consciousness (意識) as a higher ideology (理念) of modernization (近代化), thereby allowing one to stand as a single owner (主人). All opposition (對立) and conflicts that may arise on the path (路程) of modernization (近代化) are not only difficult to resolve in their essence (本體), but even if one attempts to adjust (調整) them, countless difficulties will inevitably arise. The question of whether to build expressways or provide scholarships to college students (大學生) can be endlessly debated.

However, it is difficult to make a judgment (判斷) on which will ultimately (窮極的) shorten the path (路程) of modernization (近代化). While such choices (選擇) are indeed the task (課題) of policymakers (政策決定者), they must be perceived (認識) by the citizens (國民) as equally (同一) meaningful (意味) to modernization (近代化).

Otherwise, it will be difficult to overcome the obstacles (障碍) that arise on the long and arduous journey (路程) of modernization (近代化). Regardless of whether the direction (方向) of modernization (近代化) emphasizes (重) security (安保), prioritizes industrialization (產業化), or focuses on welfare (福祉), it is our duty (責務) to protect (守護) and modernize (近代化) our own homeland (祖國). We must never forget this point (點).

Here lies the necessity (必要性) of a spiritual revolution (精神革命) as the foundation (土양) of modernization (近代化), and the reason why the Saemaul Undong, as part of the modernization movement (近代化運動), must have the character (性格) of a consciousness revolution movement (意識革命運動). The spiritual revolution (精神革命) or consciousness revolution (意識革命) is the path (路程) to modernizing (近代化) the homeland (祖國). It is because this becomes the vitality (活力素) and nourishment (養分) on the arduous and strenuous path (路程) of modernization (近代化).

## 2. Industrialization (產業化) and the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

In achieving modernization (近代化), what is urgent is not establishing new systems (制度) but the task (課業) of swiftly transforming our impoverished homeland (祖國) from a state of vicious cycles (惡循環) into a prosperous nation (富强). The slogan "The shortcut to the modernization (近代化) of the homeland (祖國) is liberation (解放) from poverty (貧困)" was strongly expressed (表現) by President Park (朴大統領) in the early 1960s with his powerful will (意志) and determination (執念), and in the 1970s (年代), it appeared as one of the guiding ideologies (指導的理念) of the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動). The Saemaul Undong (새마을運動), which aimed to shake off 5,000 years (千年) of poverty and live well, blazed as a rural modernization (農村近代化) movement (運動).


--- (p. 84) ---

Transforming the roots of our nation's poverty into roots of abundance had to begin in the countryside (農村), according to the fundamental direction that the modernization of rural areas should start with "income (所得) increase" projects and "environment (環境) improvement" projects, which then developed into a modernization movement for the entire society (社會).

Historically, humanity has continually struggled against poverty, with the majority living in poverty. Liberation from this eternal curse of humanity began to become possible only with the advent of modern history (近代史), achieved by a few Western nations through industrialization (工業化), a change in industrial structure (産業構造).

The nations swept by this wave of industrialization were largely Western societies centered around the Atlantic Ocean (大西洋), constituting only a tiny fraction of the world's population. Through two centuries of persistent effort, these nations have nearly completely escaped the historical state of poverty, earning them the title of advanced industrial nations.

From a world historical perspective, the second wave of industrialization uniquely occurred in Japan (日本). As is well known, Japan's industrialization process began nearly three centuries later than that of Western Atlantic nations, but due to its rapid, high-speed growth after World War II, it achieved remarkable records, ranking among the top advanced industrial nations.

The pressing question now is which nation will lead the third wave of industrialization in world history. Currently, only a few nations have achieved industrialization, while approximately 150 nations worldwide remain pre-industrial or are in the process of industrialization. Thus, the competition to become the protagonist of the third wave of industrialization is bound to be a fiercely competitive struggle, with those who fail facing continued historical poverty, leaving affluent living as a distant aspiration.

### Korean Industrialization (韓國的産業化) Coordinates

In general, industrialization in newly independent nations begins with a consciousness of the problem of mass poverty and its resolution.


--- (p. 85) ---

## Chapter 2: The Fundamental Spirit of Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

The urge to make a decision is rooted in the desire for industrialization, which is seen as a primary criterion for recognizing the necessity of economic poverty. In this context, industrialization as one of the goals of modernization for a newly established country emphasizes the practical resolution of urgent economic issues over the ideal of realizing an ideal society.

However, despite the reality that industrialization is an economic development issue aimed at overcoming poverty in developing countries, it occupies a central position in the path of modernization for the following three reasons.

First, for "developing countries" that have become acutely aware of the severe gap in wealth between developed and developing countries, rapid economic development is a means to truly secure independence.

Second, economic development is an indispensable prerequisite for meeting the numerous new expectations held by members of society seeking to promote modernization, such as improving living standards, spreading education, and enhancing health care.

Third, economic development is one of the fundamental elements that bring about changes in the values, motivations, and enthusiasm necessary for modernization.

Whether industrialization is seen as a practical means of liberation from poverty or as a core goal of modernization for securing independence, satisfying new expectations, and developing the necessary values and motivations for modernization, the goal of industrialization must consider the conditions under which these desires and meanings can be put into practice. While the root cause of the backwardness of newly established countries may ultimately lie in the political, economic, and cultural structures themselves, from an economic perspective, it lies in the underdevelopment of the secondary industry sector, namely, the industrial sector. It is not possible to assume that all developing countries can satisfy their desires for liberation from poverty or achieve their modernization goals through industrialization. Given the historical, geographical, humanistic, and cultural differences among developing countries, each must choose the direction and process of industrialization according to its own conditions.

Furthermore, newly established countries pursuing industrialization in circumstances different from those of advanced countries must consider who will lead this effort.


--- (p. 86) ---

There is also a serious problem with what needs to be done. The difference in "conditions" (여건) between the early stages of industrialization in advanced countries (先進國) and the situation facing newly emerging countries (新生國) today becomes even more apparent when borrowing the words of Myrdal (Gunnar Myrdal). "Newly emerging countries (新生國) are, in most cases (大部分), characterized by significantly lower economic levels (經濟水準), unfavorable ratios (比率) of population (人口) to resources (資源), and further worsening conditions (惡條件) due to rapid population growth (急激增加). Additionally, they lack outlets for emigration (移民), do not possess international capital markets (國際資本市場), and their social institutional preconditions (社會制度的前提條件), such as rationality (合理性), tradition (傳統), and laws (法律), are significantly lagging. Moreover, newly emerging countries (新生國) are latecomers (新參者) without colonies (植民地) that can be exploited as markets (市場) or sources of raw materials (原料). While the majority of the world's countries (世界) are agricultural nations (農業國), only advanced nations (先進諸國) have enjoyed and developed the advantage (利點) of being the sole industrial nations (工業國) with quasi-monopolistic benefits (準獨占的利益)."

Given the above arguments (諸論議), achieving the goals of industrialization (產業化) in the situation of Korea (韓國) requires a realistic understanding (現實的認識) of the masses' (大衆) desires (欲求) and the conditions (與件). The fact that the Republic of Korea (大韓民國) was established with the constitution (憲法) stipulating participation (參與) and distribution (配分) as the primary (一次的) national modernization (近代化) goals (目標) rather than economic (經濟) ones, indicates that there was a mistake in recognizing the popular desire (大衆的欲求) for liberation (解放) from poverty (貧困). Before accepting the realistic desire (現實的欲求) for industrialization (產業化) as "liberation (解放) from poverty (貧困)," there was an obsession (執着) with the Western-style (西歐式) political democracy (政治的民主主義) illusion (虛構), and it took more than 15 years (15年) to wake up from this illusion (虛構). Furthermore, the defects (缺陷) in power (權力) and economy (經濟) arising from the failure of political development (政治發展) to precede economic development (經濟發展) in a mixed economy (混合經濟) or public economy (公經濟) have made it impossible not to present "social purification (社會淨化)" and "elimination of irrationality (不條理剔抉)" as indispensable prerequisites (先決要件) for governance (統治) through slogans (口號) even after 30 years (30餘年).

The ultimate path to reaching the goals of industrialization (產業化) is to base it on an accurate diagnosis (正確診斷) of the masses' (大衆) desires (欲求) and an understanding (認識) of the conditions (與件). This is then consolidated (結集) into an ideology (理念) aimed at modernization (近代化).

### Rural Modernization Movement (農村近代化運動)

As part of the modernization (近代化) process of the motherland (祖國), industrialization (產業化) was fully initiated based on the recognition (認識) of national desires (國民的欲求) and the situational conditions (狀況的與件) of Korea (韓國). This culminated in the rural modernization movement (農村近代化運動) of the 1970s.


--- (p. 87) ---

## Chapter 2: The Fundamental Spirit of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) has begun. At least, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) started taking shape in the 1970s as a temporal (時點) point and chose rural areas (農村) as its spatial (場所的) selection (選擇). This was possible because there was a leader (指導者) and guiding ideology (指導的인 이념) in the 1960s (年代) who aimed for the modernization (近代化) of the fatherland (祖國).

In the early 1960s (初), former President Park Chung-hee, who had determined that the shortcut to modernization (近代化) was liberation from poverty (貧困), was grappling with the task (課題) of how and where to generate the power to escape poverty (貧困). According to the general logic (一般的 논리) of industrialization (產業化), underdeveloped countries (後進國) should develop their agriculture (農業) as a foundation (基盤) and gradually proceed with the process of industrialization (工業化) using the surplus (餘力) gained from agricultural development (農業發展). According to this method (方式), for the industrialization (工業化) of Korea (韓國), our rural areas (農村) would have to sweat and save, imposing an unbearable burden (負擔) on farmers (農民) and only after a long period of time (歲月) would the surplus (餘力) for industrialization (工業化) be generated. Given the political situation (政勢) surrounding the Korean Peninsula (韓半島) in the 1960s (年代), we did not have the temporal (時間的) leeway (餘裕) to follow such a general theory (一般理論), and we would have to endure the difficulty (困難) of finding jobs (一處) for the many university graduates (大學卒業者) in the agricultural sector (農業部門). Regarding this point (點), we must pay attention (注視) to the fact that in several countries in Southeast Asia (東南亞) today, although the number of university graduates (大學卒業者) is increasing, there are no jobs (一處) for them within the foundation (基盤) of the traditional (傳統的) rural economy (農村經濟), which is becoming a factor (要因) in social instability (社會不安).

According to the general economic theory (一般的經濟理論) of industrialization (產業化), Korea's (韓國) poverty problem (貧困問題) would have to remain in an insurmountable, cyclical theory (宿命的循環論). However, the firm belief (信念) of the late President Park (朴大統領) that modernization (近代化) of the fatherland (祖國) could not be achieved without escaping poverty (貧困), and his will (意志) to overcome poverty (貧困), led to the discovery of a breakthrough (突破口) to escape the vicious cycle (惡循環). The fruits (所產) of such will (意志) and obsession (執念) are expressed in the development (發展) of Korea (韓國) in the 1960s (年代). Truly, the first (第一次) and second (第二次) Five-Year Economic Development Plans of the 1960s (年代) were evidence (證據) of the Korean people's (韓民族) potential (底力) expressed through the strong (强한) will (意志) and obsession (執念) of the leader (指導者) in the face of negative public opinion (否定的輿論) that said, "It won't work" and "It will be difficult."

The rapid economic growth (高度成長) of Korea (韓國) achieved in the 1960s (年代) was more pronounced in cities (都市) than in rural areas (農村), and more in non-agricultural sectors (非農業部門) than in agriculture (農業). However, as the foundation (基盤) of industrialization (工業化) was established, exports (輸出) increased rapidly, and the economic activity (經濟活動) of commercial and industrial cities (商工都市) expanded, the modernization (近代化) of rural areas (農村近代化) was


--- (p. 88) ---

A driving force (底力) has emerged.

Such a force (底力) greatly enhanced the government's (政府) support (支援力) for rural development (農漁村開發). As government (政府) support (支援) for rural development (農村開發) increased year by year, the roles of the government (政府) and the villagers themselves became more distinct.

While some farmers (農民) became more dependent (依他心) on government support (政府支援) as it increased, others began to realize that rural areas (農村) could only be modernized (近代化) if the farmers (農民) took the initiative themselves. This led to the emergence of self-help movements (自力更生運動) in various places. Such phenomena became evident in the late 1960s (年代).

This fact indicates that the first driving force for rural modernization (農村近代化) in Korea was generated during the process of industrialization (工業化) of the Korean economy (經濟). However, as the force (底力) gained from industrialization (工業化) flowed into rural areas (農村), the second driving force for rural modernization (農村近代化) emerged from within the rural communities (農村內部), driven by the farmers (農民) themselves. The enduring and creative force (力) for rural modernization (農村近代化) ultimately lies in the self-help (自力更生) efforts of the farmers (農民) themselves.

The late President Park's (朴大統領) firm will (意志) and determination (執念) to modernize the nation (祖國近代化) served as the direct driving force (原動力) that ignited the passion (熱氣) of Saemaul in the hearts of the farmers (農民).

The passion (熱氣) of Saemaul, where people of all ages, both men and women, participate together to create a better homeland (祖國) and a better local community (故鄕) with their own strength (力), spread across the country like a wildfire.

The spirit (精神) of Saemaul, characterized by diligence (勤勉), self-help (自助), and cooperation (協同), reflected the true spirit (農心) of the farmers (農民).

Such spirit (農心) is the spirit (精神) of loving agriculture (愛農精神) and loving one's hometown (愛鄕精神). Agriculture (農業) is something that others cannot do for you; farmers (農民) must cultivate it themselves. Without diligence (勤勉), one cannot succeed in farming (農業). In farming, which is a battle against nature (自然), there is no room for deceit (欺瞞), so one must be sincere (誠實). Due to the small-scale management (零細經營) of farms, the only way to increase one's assets (家産) is through frugality (儉約), turning small gains into great achievements (泰山). In rural life (農村生活), mutual aid (隣保相助) and cooperation (協同) are essential.

Therefore, the spirit (精神) of self-help (自助), self-reliance (自立), diligence (勤勉), sincerity (誠實), frugality (儉約), and cooperation (協同) has been passed down through the ages in our rural communities (農村), reflecting the true spirit (農心) of the farmers (農民). However, in the modern era (近世紀), such spirit (農心) has been fading away, swept along by transient (過渡期的) trends (風潮).

# Chapter 2: The Fundamental Spirit of Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

Da. Therefore, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) can be seen as a movement for farmers to rediscover their agricultural spirit (農心) and for Korean (韓國) rural areas (農村) to rediscover their self-identity (自我).

## Da. A Movement Aiming for Prosperity

The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), encapsulated by the catchphrase "Movement for Prosperity (運動)," was a rural modernization (近代化) movement that aimed for industrialization (產業化) through income increase (所得增大) and improved productivity (生産性) via labor-management cooperation (勞使 協力), while also promoting a consciousness revolution (意識 革命) as the ultimate goal of modernization (近代化). The ideological principles (理念的 原理) that the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) aimed for in the 1970s (年代) can be summarized as follows.

First, the movement was promoted based on the recognition (認識) that it was a foundation (“터”) for industrialization (產業化).

Second, the movement was promoted with the basic needs (基本的 慾求) of the people (國民) as the primary guiding principle (第一次的 指導 原理) to achieve the goals (目標) of industrialization (產業化).

Third, the movement emphasized the interconnectedness and simultaneity (同時性) of economic construction (經濟 建設) and consciousness revolution (意識 革命) or spiritual revolution (精神 革命) in pursuing industrialization (產業化).

From the beginning, rural modernization (農村 近代化) emphasized the element (要素) of spiritual revolution (精神 革命). The Saemaul spirit (精神) of diligence (勤勉), self-help (自助), and cooperation (協同) encapsulates this. The fact that the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) involved a spiritual revolution (精神 革命) was the first reason why this movement could aim for the ultimate goal of national modernization (祖國 近代化) rather than merely pursuing superficial industrialization (外型的 產業化), and it is also what distinguishes this movement from modernization efforts (近代化 努力) in other countries (外國).

Fourth, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) had the principle (原理) of solving various problems (諸般 問題點) that inevitably arise in the early stages (初期 過程) of industrialization (產業化) through spiritual revolution (精神 革命).

Fifth, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) aimed to establish Korean (韓國的) labor-management ethics (勞使 倫理) as an immediate task (當面 課題) to achieve the goal (目標) of industrialization (產業化).

In the early stages (初期 段階) of capitalism (資本主義), labor-management relations (勞使 關係) were once perceived as solely antagonistic (對立的), but in today's mature industrial society (成熟 段階 産業 社會), mutual understanding (理解) and dialogue (對話) leading to cooperative relations (協同 關係) have become common sense (一般的 常識). Currently, Korean labor-management relations (韓國 勞使 關係) are also based on cooperative or collaborative relations (協同 協調 關係). In particular, workers (近勞者) are institutionally protected (制度的 保障) by labor relations laws (勞動 關係 法規), and through the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), they can be protected (保護) in a more natural manner (順理的).


--- (p. 90) ---

Looking back, in a society where the high degree of labor division had not yet been achieved and the standard of living was low, anyone who devoted themselves to their work could improve their own standard of living. The joy of labor and the joy of life were in perfect harmony.

However, as society transitioned into a high-industrialized one, the value of labor came to be determined not by labor itself but by the satisfaction derived from private life and leisure activities. The recognition of this shift led to the emergence of a 'social humanism' that rejected mechanistic views of humanity. The apathy of blue-collar workers engaged in production processes and the melancholy of white-collar workers in management were inevitable results of neglecting the importance of leisure, family activities, and social and spiritual pursuits. We must not repeat the maladies and vicious cycles that advanced nations have experienced and continue to experience. We need to deeply instill the Saemaul spirit of diligence, self-help, and cooperation into our corporate culture to establish a new labor-management order unique to Korea. To this end, employers must improve working conditions and strive for the welfare of employees with a deep sense of public duty and strong responsibility. Employees, in turn, must contribute to improving corporate productivity with a spirit of dedication and active participation. In companies where factory Saemaul Undong is successfully implemented, a harmonious and cooperative atmosphere akin to a family is fostered, leading to the formation of Korea's unique labor-management relations. Our traditional culture provides a foundation for such familial labor-management relations, allowing us to avoid the pitfalls of Western industrial nations grappling with labor issues. Instead, we must create labor-management relations suited to our cultural background, which is currently being realized in line with the ideological direction of industrialization as a means of modernizing our nation.

It has often been assumed that Confucian culture acts as a constraint in achieving modernization or industrialization as a process of modernization. However, at the current stage where the foundation of our economic industrialization has been laid, we must revive our traditional ideology of loving the country and serving our parents, and internalize the life ethics of patience and self-discipline underlying Confucian culture as wisdom and virtue to be respected in life.


--- (p. 91) ---

It is not acceptable. From this perspective, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) holds ideological value as it rationally integrates traditional cultural factors into Korea's modernization process as a national indicator. In other words, the Saemaul Undong is a nationalist integration into modernization.

### 3. Democratization and the Saemaul Undong

Democracy, an era-defining universal value with immense appeal today, has reigned as the sovereign political justification, captivating nearly all nations, societies, and individuals on this planet. However, even communists have appropriated the magical allure of its terminology. No other concept has been as hotly debated in the 30-odd years since World War II as democracy.

This is partly because democracy is a complex and intricate theory and institution, but also because the concept of democracy is not a finished product but rather an unfinished one. Additionally, the issue of how any institution integrates with its "place" and "time," that is, its "soil," is fundamental. Even in Western Europe, the birthplace of democracy, skepticism about democracy has emerged, and undemocratic elements can sometimes be found within those societies. In terms of institutions, the differences are stark. For instance, the political institutions of the United Kingdom and the United States are so different that they even evoke a sense of dissimilarity. Clearly, democracy is a matter of degree.

However, the difficulty of discussing democracy is not limited to the West. It is a debate, orientation, and anguish surrounding the political institutions and governing legitimacy of the citizens of newly independent nations. After World War II, many newly independent nations adopted democracy as their governing legitimacy and ideology. However, their political changes have consistently shown that democracy is a process of endless trials. Particularly, as these new nations advanced in their modernization efforts, faced new international environments, and responded to popular demands for democracy, democracy underwent immense transformations in its content. This transformation has given rise to various critical views on the operation of democracy. In the case of Korea, this trend has been almost similar. Until recently, it was the domain of a small number of intellectuals


--- (p. 92) ---

# Democratic Ideals and the Saemaul Undong

What was once merely an abstract concept, democracy (民主主義) began to take root as a constitutional reality (憲法形態) in the Republic of Korea (大韓民國) during the Cold War era (冷戰狀況下). However, as the frequent changes in our constitutional history (憲政變化) indicate, the path of our democracy (民主主義) over the past 30 years (30餘年) has been far from smooth.

Democracy (民主主義) is an indispensable national benchmark (國家指標) and the cornerstone (礎石) of national revival (民族中興). As we embark on a new era (時代), our democracy (民主主義) must spread its wings and take root. However, this requires wise (賢明) wisdom (智慧) and persistent (忍耐) patience, as well as a delicate (精巧) and meticulous (工程) process. For democracy (民主主義) to take hold in our context (「터」와「때」), the basic principles (基本原理) underlying its ideology (基本理念) and institutions (制度) must be clearly understood (認識) and internalized (生活化) by each and every citizen (國民). Moreover, the political (政治), economic (經濟), social (社會), and cultural (文化的) factors (諸要因) necessary for democracy (民主主義) must mature (成熟). To achieve this, we cannot merely wait for the future (將來); instead, deliberate (人爲的) and institutional (制度的) efforts must be organized (組織的) and implemented.

In this sense, the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) serves as a catalyst (促進劑) and a practical arena (實踐道場) for the localization (土着化) of democracy (民主主義). As we reflect on the first decade (10年) of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) and discuss its ideological (理念的) coordinates (座標) for the future (來日), democracy (民主主義) must be at the core (中核) of its guiding ideology (指導理念).

## A. The Korean Coordinates of Democracy (韓國的 좌표)

To explore what democracy (民主主義) should look like in Korea (韓國), it would be beneficial to examine the critical perspectives (批判的 견해) on the operation (運用) of our democracy (民主主義) thus far. These critiques (批判論) discuss Korean democracy (韓國에서의 민주주의) in light of the basic principles (基本原則) of Western-style (西歐式) democracy (民主主義), which is its birthplace (發祥地). Thus, they clearly present (提示) the tension (衝突) and connection (連繫) between the universal (普遍的) meaning (意味) of democracy (民主主義) and its localization (定着) in Korea (韓國).
