### Section 2: Income Augmentation Businesses (事業) of the Saemaul Undong (Movement)

#### 1. Significance of Income Augmentation Businesses (事業)

The Saemaul Undong (Movement) has been understood and expressed as a "movement for better living," that is, a movement for "not just me, but for my neighbors, my village, and all the people of the nation to live well together."
This stems from the fact that the Saemaul Undong (Movement) has taken "the rationalization (能率化) of economic (經濟) and social (社會) development (開發) and the nationwide (國民的) equitable distribution (均霑) of welfare (福祉)" as its fundamental ideology (理念), and has emphasized "diligence (勤勉), self-help (自助), and cooperation (協同)" as the best methods (方法) for realizing this ideology (理念).
The Saemaul Undong (Movement) has also attracted global (汎世界的) interest as a comprehensive rural development program (綜合農村開發事業), specifically a Korean-style (韓國的) comprehensive rural development program (綜合農村開發事業).
This is because the Saemaul Undong (Movement) has attempted comprehensive development (綜合開發) of "rural areas (農村), farmers (農民), and agriculture (農業)," and in terms of development (開發) priorities (優先順位), it has placed more emphasis on the development (開發) of rural areas (農村) rather than agriculture (農業), and on farmers (農民) rather than rural areas (農村), which is a distinctive feature of its development (開發) strategy (戰略).


--- (p. 408) ---

Thus, the "comprehensive development strategy" of improving the living environment of "rural villages (農村)"—developing the spirit of "farmers (農民)"—increasing the production of "agriculture (農業)" and enhancing the income of "farm households (農家)" brought about development results that were almost miraculous and unprecedented worldwide. As a result, the Saemaul Undong (運動) became a focal point of global interest.

The contributions and achievements of such a Saemaul Undong (運動) can be evaluated and analyzed from various perspectives depending on the viewpoint and problem awareness.

From the perspective of the initial ideology and the solution of Korean (韓國的) problems, the first achievement that should be highly evaluated is the spiritual development, that is, the great transformation in the consciousness structure of farmers (農民).

In other words, through the Saemaul Undong (運動), farmers (農民) experienced the power and results of the collective synergy advocated by Esman (a social psychologist) and achieved what Gunnar Myrdal referred to as the "revolution of rising expectations."

Next, the "rapid advancement of the Green Revolution (綠色革命)" and the achievement of "self-sufficiency in grains (米穀)" should also be highly evaluated as another achievement.

The early Saemaul Undong (運動) focused on increasing food production through the production of compost and soil improvement using imported soil. As the Saemaul Undong (運動) developed, the focus of the food production movement also shifted, placing greater emphasis on the development and expansion of high-yielding new varieties. As a result, new varieties introduced to farms starting in 1972 saw their cultivation area rapidly expand, reaching 76.2% of the total grain cultivation area by 1978. This led to a sharp increase in grain yields per unit area, surpassing Japan's level continuously from 1975. From 1976, self-sufficiency in grains was achieved, and in 1977, a world-record grain yield of 494 kg was recorded.

Thirdly, the attempt to conduct comprehensive development by village type through the Saemaul Undong (運動) and the promotion of comprehensive regional agricultural development projects at the town (邑) and district (面) levels based on this should also be evaluated as one of the major achievements.


--- (p. 409) ---

# Chapter 5 (第5章) Achievements and Results of the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動)

From the mid-1970s, as the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動) shifted its focus to income augmentation (所得增大), the government (政府) prioritized comprehensive development (綜合開發) tailored to different village types (類型別) and provided concentrated support for these initiatives.

To this end, the government (政府) first established comprehensive development directions (綜合開發方向) for villages based on their geographical characteristics, such as mountainous (山間), mid-mountainous (中山間), plains (平野), suburban (都市近郊), and fishing villages (漁村). It then encouraged the creation of self-reliant villages (自立마을) centered around a 7-year income augmentation plan (所得增大 7개년 計劃) ('75〜’81). As a result, 4,000 self-reliant villages (自立마을) developed long-term plans (長期計劃). However, due to issues such as the plans' lack of economic viability (經濟性) and feasibility (妥當性), as well as constraints in securing funds (資金調達), these plans were not implemented. Nevertheless, the process of creating these plans enabled villagers to develop their own long-term visions (vision). Moreover, it heightened farmers' (農民) interest and motivation (關心과意慾) in developing underutilized resources (遊休資源), such as upland agriculture (山地農業) and water resources (水資源). Additionally, it served as an opportunity for villagers, village leaders (村里指導者), and public officials (公務員) to learn about long-term planning (長期計劃).

Furthermore, the government (政府) renamed existing specific projects (特定事業) as New Village Income Augmentation Projects (所得增大事業) and modified their approaches, emphasizing comprehensive village-level development (單位綜合開發).

Concurrently, government agencies (政府) and related organizations (事業有關機關), such as the Interior Ministry (內務部), Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries (農水產部), National Agricultural Cooperative Federation (農協), and Rural Development Administration (農振廳), promoted model village development projects (示範마을育成事業) under various names, including outstanding (優秀), self-reliant (自立), and model (示範), to demonstrate and expand the effects of village-level comprehensive development projects (單位綜合開發事業). The hallmark of these projects was their integrated approach (一括計劃)(Package Program), encompassing various initiatives from production infrastructure improvement (生産基盤整備事業) to the expansion of production and distribution facilities (生産 • 流通施設), agricultural mechanization (農業機械化), introduction of income-generating crops (所得作目), and enhancement of cultural and welfare facilities (文化 • 福祉施設).

These model village development projects (示範마을育成事業) are analyzed as having yielded significant results (成果). Notably, the Special Agricultural Projects (農特) and New Village Income Augmentation Projects (所得增大事業) provided participating farms (參與農家) with opportunities to achieve annual average incomes (年平均 所得) 10% higher than general farms (一般農家). Additionally, the establishment of main production clusters (主産團地) accelerated the development of growth-oriented agriculture (成長農業), such as fruit, vegetable, and livestock farming (過수 • 채소 • 축산). Furthermore, these projects contributed to improving the international balance of payments (國際收支改善) through increased agricultural exports (農產物輸出).


--- (p. 410) ---

The demonstration village development project significantly contributed to increasing agricultural income. It was revealed that the average household income in these villages reached 2,228,000 won in 1979. Additionally, the project greatly contributed to the rationalization and scientification of farmers' consciousness through the active adoption of new farming techniques and the promotion of farming enthusiasm.

However, the demonstration village development project had limitations in expanding its demonstration effects and deepening the project itself due to its small scale. In other words, it was found that economic feasibility and relative advantages could not be guaranteed at the village level, ranging from the improvement of production bases to the expansion of production and circulation facilities, agricultural mechanization, and regional specialization of agricultural production.

Therefore, since 1977, regional agricultural development projects have been promoted with town and township units as the center, and as of 1979, 200 unit agricultural cooperatives are promoting this project. This project is analyzed to have a very significant effect in terms of increasing agricultural income and, in particular, the comprehensive development of regional agriculture centered on the complex development of "main + subsidiary + secondary crops."

Fourthly, it is important to evaluate the fact that the off-season period in our rural areas has disappeared through the Saemaul Undong, and accordingly, non-agricultural income has shown a sharp increase as one of the important achievements.

The fundamental reasons for the disappearance of the off-season period can be found in two aspects: the non-seasonalization of agricultural production and the increase in non-agricultural employment opportunities.

First, the promotion of non-seasonalization of agricultural production can be attributed to the concentrated promotion of various development measures such as the Saemaul Undong income increase project, the demonstration village development project, and the comprehensive regional agricultural development project at the town and township level. This has led to rapid growth in growth-oriented agriculture such as fruit, high-grade horticulture, and livestock farming.

On the other hand, the increase in non-agricultural employment opportunities can be attributed to the decentralization of factories to local areas and the concentrated promotion of various projects through the Saemaul Undong, such as the Saemaul wage increase project, the forest income increase project, the off-season production project, and the Saemaul factory construction project.

In this way, as non-agricultural employment opportunities increased, non-agricultural income also increased sharply, and in the 1970s,


--- (p. 411) ---

# Chapter 5: General Overview and Achievements of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

Initially, the proportion was less than 20%, but by 1979, it exceeded the 30% level.

This indicates that the continuous increase in farm household income was achieved through the increase in non-farm income. Such an increase in non-farm income is analyzed to have been achieved mainly through the stable provision of non-farm income sources due to the decentralization of factories to rural areas and the construction of Saemaul factories.

Fourthly, rural women actively participated in the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), leading to an increase in rural savings and the rationalization and scientification of farm household consumption life through the joint purchase of daily necessities. This fact should also be evaluated as one of the major achievements of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement).

Lastly, an important aspect to be evaluated is the method of the Saemaul projects.

The fundamental reason why various achievements mentioned earlier could be accomplished is found in the promotion method of the Saemaul projects.

Among various Saemaul project methods, particularly ① the phased comprehensive development pilot of agriculture, farmers, and rural areas, ② the phased development and promotion of Saemaul projects, ③ priority support for excellent villages, ④ mutual respect for residents' opinions, ⑤ the leading role of Saemaul leaders, and ⑥ the active participation of women have been analyzed to play a decisive role in bringing about the success of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement).

## 2. Consciousness Reform and Innovation of Living Order

### A. Revolution of Expectation and Consciousness Reform

#### (1) Spiritual Poverty and Laziness

The greatest transformation in our society achieved through the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) is the significant change in the consciousness structure of village residents. This achievement can be seen as a result of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) placing its primary goal on the development of residents' consciousness.

The reason why the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) emphasizes consciousness development is found in its problem awareness regarding the fundamental causes of poverty.

As pointed out by the world-renowned scholar Gunnar Myrdal, Western Europe, which has high interest in the economic development issues of developing countries, particularly the Southeast Asian nations,


--- (p. 412) ---

Social scientists (社會科學者) generally identify the fundamental causes of poverty (貧困) in economic (經濟的) factors (要因). A representative example is Professor Ragnar Nurkse, who points out that in developing countries (開發途上國), the vicious cycle of poverty (「빈곤(貧困)의 악순환(惡循環)」) has been repeated due to severe capital shortages (資本不足), an economic (經濟的) factor (要因).

However, the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) has approached the fundamental causes of poverty (貧困) with a different awareness (問題意識). In the case of our country, the fundamental cause of the vicious cycle of poverty (貧困의 악순환) has been more closely tied to non-economic (非經濟的) factors (要因), specifically spiritual (精神的) poverty (貧困), rather than economic (經濟的) factors (要因). This awareness (問題意識) served as the foundation for the initiation (始作) of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동).

In reality (事實上), our farmers (農民) have lived with both material (物質的) and spiritual (精神的) poverty (貧困). They lacked the spiritual (精神的) leisure (餘裕) and courage (勇氣) to honestly accept backwardness (落後), stagnation (沈滯), poverty (貧困), and ignorance (無知) as their own fault (我的責任) or responsibility (責任). They were steeped in the spiritual (精神的) bad habit (弊習) of blaming others for their poverty, attributing it solely to their ancestors (祖上), holding the government (政府) responsible for backwardness (落後) and stagnation (沈滯), and attributing the prevalence (發延) of unproductive (非生產的) bad winds (弊風) entirely to the mistakes of the leadership (指導層).

In this way, our past (過去) rural communities (農村) were characterized by backwardness (落後), stagnation (沈滯), resignation (諦念), and laziness (懶怠), and were criticized (指摘) as typical stagnant societies (停滯社會).

## (2) Promoting a Sense of Responsibility and Cooperation (責任 · 協同意識의 고취(鼓吹))

One aspect of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) that deserves high praise (評價) for its achievements (成果) is its contribution to the spiritual development (精神啓發) of the entire nation (國民).

The fact that the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) sparked a revolution (革命) of rising expectations (漸高하는 기대) within the stagnant (停滯) rural society (農村社會) is not only an achievement (成果) of the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) but also the very driving force (原動力) that led to its success (成功的). This deserves high praise (評價).

Professor Gunnar Myrdal, in his book "Asian Drama" (「아시아의 드라마(Asian Drama)」), emphasizes three aspects (側面) in the process (過程) of explaining the revolution of expectations (期待의 혁명): national (國民的) awareness (自覺), the educated stratum (敎育받은 계층), and the flow of a certain period of time (一定한 시간의 흐름).

That is, the national (國民的) awareness (自覺) that the entire nation (國民) can shape (形成) its own destiny (運命) and take responsibility (責任) for doing so is the driving force (原動力) that sparks the revolution of expectations (期待의 혁명).


--- (p. 413) ---

# Chapter 5: Achievements and Results of the Saemaul Undong (Movement)

It is said that such a revolution is limited to the educated class and that it takes a considerable amount of time for the revolution to spread to more residents and become further intensified, eventually reaching the stage of aspiring for the realization of a democratic welfare state.

The Saemaul Undong (Movement) has played a decisive role in awakening the self-awareness of all citizens, particularly farmers, and has served as the driving force for the expected revolution.

The Saemaul Undong (Movement) made farmers realize that their poverty was their own responsibility and that they could all live well through cooperation.

These facts are well supported by the results of a survey on farmers' consciousness structure regarding the objectives, promotion methods, and responsibility for the success or failure of the Saemaul Undong (Movement) (Note: Conducted in 1978 by the Rural Economic Research Institute).

According to the survey results, only less than 40% of farmers understood the Saemaul Undong (Movement) as a movement for their own benefit or for the development of their village. In contrast, more than 50% of farmers believed that it was a movement for all citizens to live well together, requiring joint efforts from all citizens and the government.

Furthermore, 35.9% of farmers felt that the responsibility for the success or failure of the Saemaul Undong (Movement) lay with themselves, while 49.5% believed that the responsibility lay with all village residents. This means that a total of 85% of farmers emphasized both their own responsibility and the shared responsibility of the village residents.

Moreover, for the efficient promotion of the Saemaul Undong (Movement), 37.2% of farmers valued the cooperation and unity of village residents over government support, and 38.5% prioritized the cultivation of village leaders. Ultimately, more than 75% of farmers emphasized self-help and cooperation among village residents.

These facts indicate that the Saemaul Undong (Movement) has played a decisive role in instilling a sense of responsibility and cooperative spirit among farmers.

### (3) Heightened Will and Expectation for Farming

Among the spiritual development effects achieved by the Saemaul Undong (Movement), the most important fact is


--- (p. 414) ---

One aspect is that it sparked a revolutionary change within rural society (農村社會), spreading rapidly. The Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) sparked a revolutionary surge in farmers' (農民) confidence (自信) and expectations (期待), with the movement's momentum revealing that they too could succeed and improve their lives. This phenomenon can be easily observed by comparing farmers' (農民) farming enthusiasm (營農意慾) and expectations (期待) levels just before the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) began in 1969 with those in 1972, when the movement had spread to nearly every village (全마을). In 1969, only 60% of farmers (農民) hoped to expand their farming scale (營農規模), but by 1972, this figure had surged to 86.8%. Additionally, the proportion of farmers (農민) expecting rural living standards (農村의 생활水準) to match or surpass urban ones (都市) jumped from 26% to 65.4%. Conversely, the percentage of farmers (農民) hoping to leave farming (離農) plummeted from 30% to 7.7%.

This revolutionary change in expectations (期待) was primarily driven by farmers (農民) with relatively lower education levels (敎育水準), contrary to expectations. This is evidenced by the fact that farmers (農民) with lower education levels (敎育水準) participated in the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) more enthusiastically (熱誠的).

According to farmers' (農民) evaluations, those who participated most enthusiastically (熱誠的) in the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동) were those with the lowest education levels (低學歴層), such as elementary school graduates (國卒), followed by those with intermediate education levels (中間學歷層), such as middle school graduates (中卒). Farmers (農民) with higher education levels (高學歴層), such as high school graduates (高卒) or above, were rather critical of or largely indifferent to the Saemaul Undong (새마을운동).

### (4) Emphasis on the Role of Women (婦女子)

In our traditional rural society (農村社會), particularly under the strong influence of Confucian (儒敎的) values (價値觀), women (女性) had a distinct ethical world and behavioral norms (行動規範) different from men (男性), often constrained by taboos (禁忌) such as "if a hen crows, the household will perish (家亡)." Women (女性) were largely confined to a plant-like existence (植物人間的), showing little interest in external changes (外界의 변화). They were expected to quietly endure all hardships within the confines of the home (家庭), diligently attending to household chores (家事), finding satisfaction (滿足) in this role, which was considered virtuous (婦徳).

Of course, even within the closed status (地位) of women (女性), figures like Shin Saimdang (申師任堂) exemplified our spiritual (精神) and literary (文) heritage.


--- (p. 415) ---

# Chapter 5 (第5章) Achievements and Results of the Saemaul Undong (運動)

Although there were women who contributed to modernization, most Korean women lived under the concepts of *samjongjideok* (三從之德) and *chilgeojiaeak* (七去之惡) and various evil customs, which cannot be denied. The Saemaul Undong (運動) not only provided women with new self-awareness and reflection but also made farmers realize the importance and necessity of women's participation in national and social development. This was a turning point.

This is evidenced by the fact that during the promotion of Saemaul Undong (事業), the opinion that women should attend village meetings (會議) and express their opinions, and actively participate in village affairs became common among both men and women. Almost 90% of men agreed that women should participate in village meetings (會議) and express their opinions, and almost 80% of farmers agreed that women should actively participate in village affairs beyond household chores. From the women's perspective, the support was even higher, with almost 93% agreeing to attend meetings (會議) and express opinions, and 82% agreeing to actively participate in village affairs.

Therefore, the Saemaul Undong (運動) served as an opportunity for women to gain new awareness of their status (地位) and for men to correctly recognize the importance of women's roles in national and social development.

## II. Development of the Saemaul Undong (事業) Promotion Model (推進方式)

### (1) Attempts at Comprehensive Development (綜合開發) of Agriculture (農業), Farmers (農民), and Rural Areas (農村)

The Saemaul Undong (運動) is particularly significant and important as a new policy attempt for the efficient development of rural areas, specifically in the aspect of "Integrated Rural Development (農村 종합개발) (Integrated Rural Development)."

In traditional agricultural policies (農政), the concept of "nong" (農), which includes agriculture (農業), farmers (農民), and rural areas (農村), has been primarily focused on the industrial function (機能) of agriculture (農業). However, the social functions (機能) from the perspectives of farmers (農民) and rural areas (農村) have been largely overlooked. As a result, agriculture (農業) has been seen as an industry with relatively low investment efficiency (投資效率), even considered a declining industry (產業). Consequently, agricultural investment (農業投資) has been avoided or underestimated, and the priority has been placed only on the development (開發) and increased production (增産) of agriculture (農業).


--- (p. 416) ---

However, the Saemaul Undong (Movement) can be seen as having begun by prioritizing the social and economic functions of rural areas and farmers over the declining industrial functions in response to the rapid advancement towards a high-industry society.

The social and economic functions of rural areas that should be particularly emphasized alongside the rapid advancement towards a high-industry society can generally be categorized as follows:

1. Role as a buffer and safety valve against rapid social change
2. Role as a breakwater against all forms of pollution derived from rapid industrialization
3. Role as a cradle for preserving indigenous traditional culture against the onslaught of foreign goods
4. Role as a spiritual resting place and mental hometown for the nation, providing greenery and emotions
5. Role as a stable supply base for national food
6. Role as a supply base for skilled labor for industrialization and a market for industrial goods

The Saemaul Undong (Movement) set the priority for rural development in the opposite direction from previous agricultural policies, emphasizing the development of rural areas over farmers, and farmers over agriculture. This approach has been supported by the fact that Saemaul projects have been carried out in a step-by-step process: improving the living environment in rural areas, cultivating the spirit of farmers, and increasing agricultural production and income.

This comprehensive approach to the development of rural areas, farmers, and agriculture by the Saemaul Undong (Movement) has ignited and spread a revolution of hope within the stagnant rural society, particularly among farmers with low education levels, and has promoted both qualitative and quantitative changes. The fact that the improvement of the living environment, which had always been at the bottom of the investment priority list, has risen to the top investment priority, and that the will of farmers, who had been forced to accept strong agricultural policies and increase production, has been transformed into a sense of ownership of their village and regional society, signifies a revolutionary turn in policy methods. This has also had nearly revolutionary effects in promoting new awareness, reflection, and vigor among farmers.


--- (p. 417) ---

### (2) Step-by-Step Development and Promotion of Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) Projects

One of the fundamental reasons why the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) could instill in farmers' consciousness, within a short period, the confidence (自信), motivation (意慾), passion (熱望), and expectations (期待) that "we can do it too, we can live well too" can be found in the approach of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) projects, which involved step-by-step development (段階的開發) and promotion (推進).

In other words, one of the reasons can be found in the fact that projects that were easy to implement, required less financial burden (資金負擔), involved less risk (危險負擔), and thus had a higher chance of success (成功可能性) were prioritized (優先的) for development (開發) and promotion (推進).

Environmental improvement projects (環境改善事業) in the initial stages (初期段階) focused on basic and easy environmental improvements (環境改善) such as improving roofs, fixing fences, widening village alleys, and beautifying small streams. The construction of community centers (會舘) and the installation of bathhouses, which are cultural and welfare facilities (文化福祉施設), were promoted as key projects (力點事業) in the next stage (段階). Housing improvement (住宅改良) and the improvement of village structures (聚落構造), which required more funds (資金) and higher-level technologies (技術), were only promoted as key projects (重點的) from the latter half of the 1970s (70年代).

Moreover, production and income-increasing projects (生産•所得增大事業), which began to be prioritized (力點) from the mid-1970s (70年代), were also initially promoted by prioritizing easy projects (事業) such as compost production, soil improvement (客土), and seasonal farming (時限營農).

Comprehensive development projects (綜合開發事業) tailored to different village types (類型別), which took into account locational conditions (立地的與件), regional characteristics (地域的特性), and the potential for developing existing resources (賦存資源), were attempted starting in 1975 (75年). Furthermore, comprehensive development projects (單位綜合開發事業) at the town (邑) and township (面) levels, which emphasized economies of scale (規模經濟性), specifically the Saemaul Income Comprehensive Development Project (所得綜合開發事業), began to be promoted starting in 1977 (77年).

In other words, this means that the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) projects started from the stage of labor cooperation (勞動協同), gradually developed into technical cooperation (技術協同), and eventually evolved into capital cooperation (資本協同).

In this way, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) projects began with easy projects (事業) and, based on the accumulated experience (經驗), technology (技術), and self-help (自助) and cooperative spirit (協同精神) gained from these, promoted projects that required more funds (資金) and higher-level technologies (技術) in a step-by-step manner (段階的). As a result, the trial-and-error aspects (試行錯誤的) were significantly reduced, while the achievements (成果) grew beyond expectations (期待).


--- (p. 418) ---

As a result, it can be inferred that the farmers' confidence, motivation, and expectations surged rapidly. This is supported by the fact that nearly 85% of farmers evaluated that the achievements of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) met their expectations.

### (3) Priority Support for Excellent Villages

Another fundamental reason why the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) could rapidly spread a revolutionary expectation within the stagnant rural society was found in the government's support method for the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement).

The Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) has generally been promoted through a five-stage process: ① ignition and stimulation through government support (政府支援), ② project selection through village assemblies (마을總會), ③ planning, ④ cooperative efforts to promote the project, and ⑤ completion and post-management of the project.

In the first stage of promoting the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), the government has supported basic materials such as cement and reinforcing bars. This support served as an opportunity to stimulate the residents' motivation and expectations, and in the process of jointly managing the supported materials and thinking about the village projects to be promoted in the future, a sense of community ("we") began to sprout in the residents' consciousness.

Furthermore, the principle of prioritizing support for villages with vigorous self-help spirit, participation consciousness, cooperation, unity, and labor spirit has played a decisive role in fostering a sense of community and triggering benevolent competition among villages.

According to recent rural society surveys, nearly 80% of farmers participated in the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) to develop their village, gain honor, and avoid falling behind neighboring villages. In contrast, only less than 10% of farmers participated due to continuous instructions and encouragement from the government and leaders, or because of the gaze and reputation of village people. Moreover, 70% of farmers participated in the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) until the end, aiming to do better than their neighboring villages.

These facts indicate that the government's priority support for excellent villages in its support method for the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)


--- (p. 419) ---

## Chapter 5 Achievements and Results of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

This indicates that the sense of community and competitive spirit among the villagers were fostered, and as a result, the Saemaul Undong (運動) spread even more rapidly.

### (4) Mutual Respect for Residents' Opinions

Another factor that should be evaluated as a key to the success of the Saemaul Undong (運動) in terms of its methodology is the maximum respect for residents' opinions.

From the selection of projects to the planning and implementation of these projects, the government has maximally respected the opinions of the residents throughout the entire process. Moreover, it has been revealed that the residents themselves have also maximally respected each other's opinions.

First, looking at the process of selecting Saemaul projects, it has been revealed that almost all villagers, rather than external instructions or recommendations, participate in the village general assembly where almost all villagers attend, and the villagers themselves decide on almost all Saemaul projects.

The attendance rate of residents at the village general assembly is almost 95%, and even residents who attend every single meeting without fail account for almost 70%. In this way, it has been revealed that projects are selected based on the consensus of residents at the village general assembly where almost all residents attend. Almost 60% of farmers say that this is the case, and less than 37% of farmers say that projects are decided by adjusting the opinions of the residents and the government to about half each.

Furthermore, almost 80% of farmers evaluate that most Saemaul projects were projects that satisfied the long-cherished wishes of the residents.

These facts can be seen as evidence that the government has maximally respected the opinions of the residents in the process of selecting Saemaul projects.

Next, it has been revealed that in the process of planning and implementing projects, the residents themselves have also maximally respected each other's opinions.

When promoting projects, there are countless cases where residents' opinions clash due to problems such as securing additional funds, materials, and manpower through their own efforts, securing necessary land, and how to allocate these among individual farming households.

In such cases, if there is even a minority opinion opposing, 86% of farmers say that it was sufficiently discussed, and only 6% of farmers say that it was almost ignored.


--- (p. 420) ---

It is evident that in resolving conflicts of interest or differing opinions among residents, mutual persuasion and consensus among all residents were prioritized, followed by mediation by village leaders, and lastly, resolution by majority vote.

In this way, the government respected the will of the residents throughout the process of promoting the Saemaul Undong, and the residents themselves also respected each other's opinions, which contributed to the successful promotion of the Saemaul Undong and further enhanced the residents' sense of self-discipline, spirit of compromise, and cooperative spirit.

### (5) The Leading Role of Saemaul Leaders

The fact that Saemaul leaders played a leading role in the process of promoting the Saemaul Undong should also be evaluated as another success factor in terms of the method of the project.

Regarding the Saemaul Undong, the government has only played a limited role as an advisor, supporter, and educator. From the spiritual development of the residents to the unity of the residents, improving the relationship between village residents and public officials, solving long-standing village issues, and developing and managing income-generating projects, almost all Saemaul Undong projects have been promoted under the leadership of Saemaul leaders.

In other words, Saemaul leaders have taken on almost all-encompassing roles, ranging from educational roles to mediation, representation, technology dissemination, project planning, execution, and management.

Regarding the almost all-encompassing roles of these Saemaul leaders, almost 60% of farmers have given positive evaluations, while only about 10% of farmers have given extremely negative evaluations.

The fundamental reason why more than half of the farmers have shown favorable and positive reactions to the role of Saemaul leaders is that most Saemaul leaders were elected by the residents, and most of the elected leaders were pure farmers who considered agriculture as their vocation.

The method of selecting Saemaul leaders is such that almost 80% of them are elected either by village resident elections or by recommendation or volunteerism from village residents.

In terms of characteristics, almost 80% of the leaders have experience as past village leaders.


--- (p. 421) ---

## Chapter 5 (第5篇) Achievements and Results of the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動)

Apart from urban living (都市生活) or overseas employment (國外就業), public service (公職), etc., they had no experience (經驗) at all, being pure farmers (農民) with an education level (敎育水準) that was mostly high school graduates (高卒) or middle school graduates (中卒).

Saemaul leaders (指導者) also revealed that, in the process of promoting Saemaul projects (新村事業), they respected the will of the village leaders (有志) more than their own will (意思), and the will of the village leaders (有志) more than the will of the entire village community (住民全體). (See Table 17)

This phenomenon (現象) can be seen as a result of the leaders (指導者) themselves experiencing the hardships (苦衷) and difficulties (隘路), and the accumulated grievances (不滿) of being farmers (農民). In this way, Saemaul leaders (指導者) were elected (選出) by the residents (住民) and, due to their purely farmer-like (農民的) attributes (屬性), they have always respected the will (意思) of the residents (住民) to the utmost (最大) in the process of promoting Saemaul projects (事業推進過程). Furthermore, in the process of improving relations (關係改善過程) between residents (住民) and public officials (公務員), they have actively represented (代辯) the will (意思) of the residents (住民), leading to positive (肯定的) and favorable (好意的) reactions (反應) from the residents (住民).

### (6) Active Participation of Women (婦女子)

Women (婦女子) in rural areas (農村), who were once thought to be the epitome of virtue (婦德) by merely taking care of household chores (安房事) and keeping the kitchen tidy (廚房事), have actively participated (參與) in the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動) by stepping out of their homes (安房) and into the village workplaces (事業場). This fact (事實) should be evaluated (評價) as one of the factors (要因) that contributed to the success (成功) of the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動). When the fiery spirit (熱情) of the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動) spread throughout our rural areas (農村), the group (階層) that welcomed (歡迎) it the most and eagerly anticipated (期待) its successful promotion (推進) was the women's group (婦女階層).


--- (p. 422) ---

Some passive male (男性) perceptions were transformed by the efforts of women (婦女子). We have encountered many self-evident (資證的) cases like this in the successful examples of the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動) that have been presented whenever the opportunity (機會) arose.

Under the belief that our prolonged (數千年) cycle of poverty (貧困) was not solely due to our lack of resources (資源不足) or circumstances (與件), but rather a lack of effort (努力), rural women (農村婦女子) have awakened the development aspirations (開發意慾) of dormant (睡眠) residents and supported the successful implementation of the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動).

In other words, women (婦女子) from all villages united with a fervent desire (慾求) to try, inspiring men (男子) and playing the role of a tow truck (牽引車) in leading the initial (初期) Saemaul Undong (새마을運動) to success (成功).

This fact indicates that rural women (農村婦女子) have not only gradually participated (參與) actively in the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動), but their participation (參與) has also become one of the key factors (要因) in the success (成功) of the movement (運動).

## Women's (婦女子) Participation (參與) and Innovation (革新) in Consumption (消費生活)

### (1) Participation (參與) of Rural Women (農村婦女子)

With the spread (擴散) of the Saemaul Undong (새마을運動) and the daily life (生活化) of the Saemaul spirit (새마을精神) as a catalyst (契機), the lifestyle order (生活秩序) and atmosphere (生活氣風) of rural society (農村社會) began to change significantly (始作).

Deep-rooted (痼疾的) gambling and superstition (迷信) from thousands of years (數千年) gradually lost their foothold, and taverns (酒廛) within the village began to disappear.

This rationalization (合理化) and scientification (科學化) of rural life (農村生活) was mainly led (主導) by rural women (農村婦女子).

Women (婦女子), not to be outdone by men (男子), provided labor (勞動力) at village work sites (事業場) and actively promoted new lifestyle movements (生活運動) through women's associations (婦人會).

From movements (運動) to rationalize (合理化) life, such as eliminating drinking (音酒) and gambling (賭博) and wearing work clothes (工作服), to simplifying (簡素化) family rituals (家庭儀禮) like reducing anniversary (回甲) and funeral (喪禮) expenses (費), and further to savings (貯蓄) movements (運動) through rice saving (節米) and joint savings (共同積金), and daily necessities (日用品) joint purchasing (共同購買) movements (運動) for buying quality (良質) and low-cost (低廉) necessities (生必品), and operating (運營) communal kitchens (共同炊事場) to aid farming (營農作業), rural households (農家) have carried out new lifestyle movements (生活運動) across all aspects (全般) of life (生活).

Among these, the daily necessities (日用品) joint purchasing (共同購買) and savings (貯蓄) movements (運動) were particularly successful (成果).


--- (p. 423) ---

## Chapter 5 Achievements and Results of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

Evaluation is possible, and the operational achievements of communal kitchens (共同炊事場) cannot be overlooked either. The operation of communal kitchens (共同炊事場) aimed to provide meals such as lunch and snacks to farmers participating in communal work, thereby improving dietary life and saving costs, while also reducing the workload of housewives to support farming activities more efficiently.

The operation of communal kitchens (共同炊事場) began in the fiscal year of 1973 and has since continued to grow, with approximately 6,000 women's organizations (婦女會), or 16% of the total 36,067 organizations, currently establishing and operating them as of the fiscal year of 1979. In terms of operational achievements, in the fiscal year of 1979, the average number of operational days per communal kitchen (共同炊事場) was 25 days, with approximately 500 people participating in cooking.

### (2) The Significance of Joint Purchasing of Daily Necessities (日用品)

Before the 1960s, when most farming households (農家) had incomes below the minimum household expenditure level, there was little need or room for rationalizing consumption life. However, as farming household (農家) income levels began to rise significantly from the early 1970s, the need and potential for rationalizing farming household (農家) consumption life gradually increased. Taking this as an opportunity, the National Agricultural Cooperative Federation (農協) began to focus on rationalizing the consumption of daily necessities (日用品) and started opening cooperative chain stores (連鎖店) in rural areas from 1970. Concurrently, as part of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement), the push for rationalizing rural life (農村生活) intensified, further accelerating the cooperative's (農協) daily necessities (日用品) supply business (事業). Particularly, with the increased role of rural women (農村婦女子) in rural development (農村開發) and the strengthening and activation of the organization of the Saemaul Women's Clubs (새마을婦女會), the cooperative purchasing and selling business (購販場) was adopted as one of the four fundamental businesses (基本事業) of the Saemaul Women's Clubs (새마을婦女會) starting in 1975. From this point, the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) and the business of improving rural daily necessities (農村日用品) consumption life (消費生活) began to be formally connected.

### (3) Cooperative Chain Stores (連鎖店) and Saemaul Purchasing and Selling Places (購販場)

Following the opening of the first cooperative chain store (連鎖店) in Jangho-won (長湖院), Gyeonggi-do (京畿道) in early 1970, the number of stores and the scale of daily necessities (日用品) supply rapidly expanded, reaching 1,483 stores and a supply scale of 64.6 billion won (圓) by 1979. A major factor supporting this rapid business expansion was the operation of the Saemaul Women's Clubs (새마을婦女會).


--- (p. 424) ---

## A Decade of the Saemaul Undong (1970-1979)

The Saemaul sales outlets (販賣) were linked with the nationwide agricultural cooperative chain stores (農協連鎖店), enabling them to serve as a bridge between the chain stores and distant farm households (農家). With over 20,000 Saemaul sales outlets established across the country, primarily in village units, and connected to the agricultural cooperative chain stores located mainly in the town centers, the utilization rate of farm households located far from the chain stores was significantly improved.

#### (4) Improvement of Daily Necessities Purchasing in Rural Areas

Due to data limitations, yearly comparisons cannot be made, but the market share of agricultural cooperative chain stores in rural areas' total expenditure on daily necessities increased from 37.6% in 1977 to 40.1% in 1978. This improvement in market share has enhanced the influence of agricultural cooperative chain stores on other daily necessities retailers in rural areas, leading to a significant price control effect on other shops in rural regions.

According to a 1978 survey by the agricultural cooperatives, the distribution margin rate for daily necessities in rural areas without agricultural cooperative chain stores was 27.5%, compared to 11.9% for agricultural cooperative chain stores. In areas with agricultural cooperative chain stores, the margin rate for similar shops was 20.3%, which is 7.2% lower than in areas without chain stores.

The direct effect of agricultural cooperative chain stores is defined as the farm household benefits derived from the price difference between the supply price of chain stores and the local market price. The indirect effect is the farm household benefits resulting from the reduction in supply prices of local shops due to the presence of chain stores. In 1978, the direct effect was 46 billion won, and the indirect effect was 987 billion won (Reference: Investigation Report on the Operational Status of Chain Stores by the Investigation Department of the National Agricultural Cooperative Federation (農協中央會)).

### La. Increase in Rural Savings

#### (1) Saemaul Undong and Rural Savings

If the ultimate goal of income increase is to improve living standards, then increased income leads to an expansion of consumption scale. However, increased income does not solely translate into consumption, as part of it is saved.


--- (p. 425) ---

# Chapter 5: Achievements and Results of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

When income levels are low, securing the resources required for increasing income becomes difficult.

Therefore, from the perspective of developing countries, it is ironically concluded that the need for savings is greater precisely because there is a lack of savings resources (due to low income). In fact, one of the driving forces behind the economic recovery of West Germany and Japan after World War II was their high national savings propensity.

The Saemaul Undong ultimately aims to increase farm income, and from 1975, the frugality movement, along with the production increase and neighborhood watch movements, became one of the three pillars of the Saemaul Undong. As it developed into a nationwide movement, it greatly helped to foster a savings culture in rural areas.

To promote a savings culture in rural areas, the primary focus was on raising farmers' awareness of savings and making savings a part of daily life.

Given the experiences of high inflation rates following liberation (August 15) and the Korean War (June 25), as well as traditional practices, there was a tendency to hoard surplus or temporary spare funds rather than save them. Correcting this misconception about savings became an urgent priority.

The second direction of promotion focused on women, whose status had improved due to changes in rural social structures and agricultural management, and centered on them for savings promotion activities. Thirdly, the rural savings network was expanded and established to every corner of rural areas to provide convenience for farmers' savings and to create a savings atmosphere.

## (2) Village Savings Banks

Village savings banks, which began in the early 1960s as part of the national reconstruction movement, are special organizations that target the entire nation, including urban and rural areas. They operate at the regional, workplace, and organizational levels, with the main purpose of creating and circulating funds among members.

While they are similar to credit cooperatives in terms of mutual aid among members, they differ in aspects such as the allocation of usage amounts, investment returns, and management. The legal basis for their establishment is the Credit Cooperatives Act.

Although village savings banks began in 1964, the national reconstruction movement itself had already started earlier.


--- (p. 426) ---

Due to not having seen the war, at the end of 1970, the number of members was 371,000, the number of village savings banks was 10,110, and the amount of deposits received was only 265 million won.

After that, in 1972, the village savings bank business was included in the 20 standard businesses of the Saemaul Undong, and with the legal basis being established under the Credit Cooperatives Act, from 1973, rapid growth was repeated, and the quantitative growth of village savings banks reached 42,436 in 1977.

After that, from 1978, with the goal of qualitative improvement, the consolidation of non-performing savings banks was promoted, resulting in a continuous decrease in the number of village savings banks. However, the total fund-raising scale centered on the number of members, capital contributions, deposits, and savings continued to grow, reaching 8.26 million members and 48.71 billion won as of September 1980.

Looking at the regional distribution of Saemaul savings banks, about 10% of the savings banks are established in urban areas, and the majority are concentrated in rural areas. In terms of savings bank units, in urban areas, they are centered around workplaces and organizations, while in rural areas, they are established centered around the village and neighborhood units, not workplaces or organizations.

### (3) Promotion of Mutual Finance and Achievement of 1 Trillion Won Savings in Rural Areas

The agricultural cooperatives, which were established in village and neighborhood units and were nominally insignificant due to their small scale, began to be treated as one of the core businesses of the cooperative period from 1969, as they were integrated into town and district units. Mutual finance aims to foster the thrift and savings spirit of farmers, to raise farming funds and other funds needed by farming households within the rural areas, to eliminate rural usury, and to establish the self-reliance base of the unit agricultural cooperatives. In 1972, large-scale integration was completed, and all unit cooperatives began to handle mutual finance. With the thrift and savings spirit of farmers promoted by the Saemaul Undong, along with the increased income of farming households, the conditions for a significant increase in rural savings were created.


--- (p. 427) ---

## Chapter 5: The Thrift and Achievements of the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement)

The savings of rural communities began to increase. By 1974, a campaign to promote savings of 1 trillion won in rural areas was launched. The content of this campaign aimed to combine the mutual finance of the National Agricultural Cooperative Federation (Nonghyup), the savings of farmers in county cooperatives, investments, and mutual aid contributions with postal savings managed by the Ministry of Communications. The goal was to increase savings from 162.1 billion won at the end of 1973 to 11,165 billion won by the end of 1980, a seven-year period.

The core role in the campaign to promote savings of 1 trillion won in rural areas was played by the cooperative system of Nonghyup. This system included the 1 trillion won savings bank, whose members were the women of the Saemaul Women's Association. The primary function of this bank was to achieve the savings target without any setbacks and to shorten the distance between cooperative members and the cooperative office, which had become distant due to the merger of units at the town and county levels. The bank was established on a natural village basis.

The 1 trillion won savings bank primarily handled the deposit and loan business of mutual finance for cooperative units, as well as small-scale credit transactions. Thanks to the expansion of such transaction organizations, the diversification of deposit types, and favorable interest rates and tax benefits, remarkable growth was achieved.

From 1972 to the end of July 1980, deposits in mutual finance increased from 13.2 billion won to 722.1 billion won, and loans increased from 12.9 billion won to 589.2 billion won. During this period, the average growth rate of deposits was 75%, which was higher than the growth rate of deposits in other financial institutions.

## A Decade of the Saemaul Undong (1970-1980)

With an average annual growth rate of 33%, the growth rate was more than twice as high.

With such rapid growth in mutual finance as its backbone, the goal of the savings campaign in rural areas, which aimed to raise one trillion won, was achieved one year ahead of the target year of 1980, in 1979. Moreover, the momentum continued, and the campaign to increase savings in rural areas persisted in 1980.

(4) Effects and Current Tasks of Increased Savings in Rural Areas
The performance of village banks and the National Agricultural Cooperative Federation's mutual finance, among others, improved significantly. This can be attributed to increased farm household income and, on the other hand, an increased savings propensity among farm households.

When comparing the savings propensity of farm households before and after the Saemaul Undong, the average savings propensity from 1968 to 1970 was only 17.6%. However, in the most recent three years, from 1976 to 1978, the average savings propensity increased to 30.3%, nearly doubling. This indicates the indirect contribution of the Saemaul Undong in fostering a savings-oriented atmosphere among farm households.

Examining the increased rural savings from the perspective of farm households, the proportion of farm financial assets (deposits, insurance, capital contributions, bonds, loans, etc.) to farm household income has been rising. Moreover, within financial assets, the proportion of institutional financial assets (including mutual finance) has significantly increased compared to private financial assets, showing a very healthy trend. Specifically, the proportion of financial assets to farm household income increased from 16.7% in 1971 to 28.3% in 1978. Meanwhile, the proportion of institutional financial assets within total financial assets increased from 49.2% to 66.1% over the same period. (Nonghyup Central Union, Farm Credit Structure and Directions for Improving Agricultural Finance, Survey Data '79-5, p51~52)

# Chapter 5: Achievements and Results of the Saemaul Undong

As a result of the increase in rural savings, the rate of farmers' private debt decreased significantly from 66.4% in 1971 to 36.7% in 1978, a reduction of 29.7 percentage points. Concurrently, rural private loan interest rates fell from an annual rate of 53% to 36% over the same period. The direct benefits to farmers from lower interest rates on mutual financial institution and village savings bank loans, which are cheaper than private loan rates, combined with the indirect effects of reduced private loan rates due to the establishment of rural savings organizations, have resulted in substantial benefits for farmers. According to a Nonghyup (National Agricultural Cooperative Federation) estimate, the reduction in direct interest burdens for farmers from mutual financial institutions alone amounted to 45.5 billion won in 1979.

While the significant effects of increased rural savings can be attributed to the diversification and quantitative expansion of savings promotion organizations and outlets, there are concerns about excessive competition among multiple savings organizations within a single village unit, which can harm the total welfare of residents and potentially lead to the emergence of problematic savings institutions.

In particular, the lower-tier organizations of mutual financial institutions, such as the 100 million won savings banks and village savings banks, are almost universally established in rural villages. Regardless of their form, there is a need for organizational coordination and the establishment of a system for business cooperation to improve relationships and comprehensively improve the system.

D. Cultivating Successors for Agriculture
(1) Cultivating Saemaul Youth Associations
(a) The Development Process of 4-H Clubs
The origins of the 4-H movement in our country can be traced back to a rural youth movement introduced by Christians during the late Japanese colonial period. However, the formal activities of 4-H began after liberation (August 15, 1945) in the Gyeonggi Province region.

At that time, the decision to promote the successful 4-H movement from the United States within the province was made with the introduction of Colonel C.A. Anderson, who served as an advisor to the Gyeonggi Province governor. Governor Gu Ja-ok of Gyeonggi Province took the lead in advancing this movement, which led to the emergence of rural youth activities in our country.

The 4-H cultivation project, which was just beginning to take root, suffered a critical blow during the Korean War (June 25, 1950), even leading to a temporary halt in the project. However, this period also provided an opportunity to spread the project nationwide.


--- (p. 430) ---

Taking the establishment of the Agricultural Affairs Institute in 1957 as an opportunity, the nationwide promotion system for agricultural education guidance was established as part of agricultural education guidance work. A Youth Affairs Division was set up at the central level to oversee youth work in rural areas, and systematic organizations were expanded at the provincial and city/county levels.

After the May 16 Revolution, the establishment of the Rural Development Agency in 1962 led to significant developments in rural youth guidance work, not only in terms of organization but also in terms of the content and scale of activities.

Following the full-scale launch of the Saemaul Undong in 1971, rural youth guidance work diversified to meet the multifaceted needs of society. Efforts were made to develop Saemaul volunteer activities and production income-increasing task activities. Members' production task activities achieved remarkable results, surpassing the production records of established farmers and playing a pioneering role in the dissemination of new technologies.

In 1977, to promote and implement the Saemaul Undong, general agricultural education was combined with Saemaul spirit education to foster the establishment of youth with a correct national perspective.

In 1978, the 4-H Promotion Enhancement Plan was drafted and approved by President Park. The President instructed that the Saemaul Undong and youth work be integrated and promoted, changing the name of 4-H clubs to Saemaul Youth Clubs and reorganizing the structure into two branches based on age.

(Organization and Business Content)

The Saemaul Youth Club work targeting rural youth is based on the ideals of wisdom, virtue, labor, and physical fitness. Through practical education, it aims to cultivate personality and hone skills to enhance the national qualities of democratic society. The guidance direction of the Saemaul Youth Work, which has been promoted under such basic goals, has changed its content according to the changes in the times. In the early 1960s, the focus was on improving the qualities of capable farmers, but in the latter half, the focus shifted to fostering second-generation farmers with a sense of the new era. In the early 1970s, the focus was on fostering future rural mid-level leaders, and in the latter half of the 1970s, the focus began to shift to fostering successor Saemaul leaders.

In this way, the content of the focal guidance direction has frequently changed according to the changes in the times.


--- (p. 431) ---

The business contents (事業內容) of the Saemaul Youth Club (靑少年會) prioritize members' (會員) task activities (課題活動), which include both individual tasks (個人課題) and group tasks (團體課題). Rural guidance agencies (農村指導機關) guide members (會員) to annually select tasks (課題) related to agricultural improvement (農事改良), life improvement (生活改善), and social life (社會生活), and to complete (履修) these tasks through their own efforts.

For younger members (年少會員), tasks (課題) such as volunteer activities (奉仕活動) or basic agricultural tasks (基礎營農課題) are selected, while for older members (年長會員), support is provided to focus on tasks (課題) that are technically more advanced and aimed at increasing production and income (所得增大課題).

Among the members (會員) of the Saemaul Youth Club (靑少年會), many have received praise (稱頌) from residents for achieving record-breaking yields (多收穫) or high incomes (所得) through task activities (課題活動). Notable examples include:

Kim Seung-ho (金勝鎬) from Boeun County, Chungbuk, who set a record of 766 kg per segment (段當) in the rice task (課題) and received the Silver Tower Industrial Medal (銀塔産業勳章) as the youngest participant (最年少者) at the National Saemaul Leaders (指導者) Conference; Son Jae-soo (孫載秀) from Changwon, Gyeongnam, who in 1970 achieved the highest nationwide yield (多收穫) in the rice task (課題), surpassing general adults (一般成人); and Lee Jae-u (李在佑), a female member (女子會員) from Okcheon, Chungbuk, who completed a task (課題) on high-degree utilization (高度活用) of cultivated land (耕地) and achieved an income (所得) of 975,000 won per 10 a (10a당).

Additionally, in 1977, Kim Young-rae (金永來) from Myeongju, Gangwon, completed a task (課題) on Hanwoo (韓牛) fattening (肥肉) and raised 11 head (頭) of Hanwoo (韓牛) per year (年).

There are countless success stories, such as achieving an income of 2,838,000 won through three deliveries.

### (d) Business Achievements
The Saemaul Youth Movement in our country has had a significant impact not only on social education for rural youth but also on the social and industrial development of rural areas. One of the major factors contributing to the successful implementation of the Saemaul Undong is the experience gained from Saemaul Youth Club activities and the pivotal roles played by many Saemaul Youth Club alumni in society. This is not an overstatement. For instance, as of the end of 1977, 9,400 Saemaul Youth Club alumni were serving as Saemaul leaders, and there were over 13,600 Saemaul agricultural technicians. Additionally, the activities of the Saemaul Youth Club have played a pioneering role in eliminating outdated customs and feudal lifestyles in rural areas, promoting rural modernization, and fostering excellent national qualities, healthy thinking, diligence, self-help spirit, and cooperative spirit.

Now, let's examine the impact of Saemaul Youth Club activities on agricultural income based on a report analyzed by the Rural Development Administration in 1975. When comparing the per-unit agricultural income of Saemaul Youth Club alumni households with that of general farming households, the per-unit agricultural income of alumni households is 26,271 won, while that of general farming households is 10,581 won, which is less than half.

### (라) Cultivation Measures (育成方案)

Just as the future of a nation depends on the spirit of its youth, it would not be an overstatement to say that the future of rural areas depends on the qualities and farming aspirations of rural youth.

However, what is the current situation in our country's rural areas? The number of people leaving agriculture in recent years has reached 400,000 to 500,000 annually, and in 1978, it peaked at 781,000. The fact that the proportion of young and middle-aged people among those leaving agriculture is increasing is a serious problem for the future of our rural areas.

Looking at the current farming conditions, we can see that the rural workforce is decreasing both quantitatively and qualitatively, and the cost of rural labor is rising rapidly, putting it in a very unfavorable situation.

Moreover, the consciousness structure of rural youth is changing to a trend of leaving the countryside and unconditionally heading towards cities, which is a concern. According to data analyzed by the National Agricultural Cooperative Federation (農協中央會) in 1978, only 13% of parents currently engaged in farming are willing to encourage or cooperate with their children to farm, while 85% of parents either encourage their children to choose other occupations or leave it up to their children's discretion.

Given that farming conditions are unfavorable and the consciousness structure regarding agriculture is changing, the need to cultivate successors for farming has become urgent. The following are the measures for cultivating successors currently being promoted or planned by the government.

First, expand the Saemaul Youth Association to all 36,000 Saemaul villages and promote autonomous activities, using Saemaul Youth Association members as the core to cultivate successors for farming.

Second, to boost the morale of Saemaul Youth Association members and strengthen practical support, expanding the fund is a top priority. To this end, the government has set a target of increasing the central-level fund, which was only 600 million won as of the end of 1979, to 10 billion won, and each provincial (道單位) and city/county (市•郡) level also aims to raise 50 billion won each as a target.


--- (p. 436) ---

Thirdly, to strengthen spiritual and material support, sisterhood ties were promoted between 193 agricultural and fishery-related companies and 228 Saemaul Youth Clubs. Requests for cooperation in these sisterhood ties were also made to the Korea Young Men's Christian Association, which had already established sisterhood ties with 195 Saemaul Youth Clubs, and to other social service organizations such as the Korean Lions Club.

Fourthly, to boost the morale of members, measures are being considered by relevant agencies to specially recruit, for a certain period, members of Saemaul Youth Clubs who, despite not having received regular higher education due to family circumstances or other reasons, lead honest, diligent, and outstanding member lives. These members would be employed by agricultural cooperatives, rural guidance centers, or township offices.

Fifthly, outstanding members and leaders who have made remarkable contributions to the guidance of Saemaul Youth will be discovered nationwide and rewarded to encourage both members and leaders.

Sixthly, there are plans to improve central-level events that have been reward-focused and to strengthen township-level competitions, camping events, and sports events to expand members' participation opportunities. The policy is to guide Saemaul Youth Club activities in a healthy direction through achievements presentations, case exchanges, physical and mental training, and cooperative living training.

Finally, the Saemaul Youth Central Training Institute plans to conduct short-term commissioned education for 2,000 people annually, and the Canaan Agricultural Military School for 3,000 people annually, to promote spiritual education that fosters loyalty and filial piety, love for agriculture, and love for the hometown. Additionally, annual training for 1,300 people at Doknong Family Farms and other agricultural skill training will be conducted in parallel.

(2) Promoting the settlement of agricultural college graduates in farming
Among the 80,000 students currently enrolled in 119 agricultural high schools nationwide, outstanding agricultural high school students with a clear intention to settle in farming after graduation have been granted full scholarships equivalent to the amount of their public contribution fees. Agricultural cooperatives, rural guidance centers, land improvement associations, and other related agencies are providing on-the-job training, and standard and personal farming design education is being conducted for all agricultural high school students. In particular, starting from the fiscal year 1980, 10 model agricultural high schools will be selected nationwide to establish independent farming departments.

### 3. Rapid Advancement of the Green Revolution (綠色革命) and Agricultural Increase (農業增產)

#### a. Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) and Agricultural Increase (農業增產)

Over the past 10 years, our country's agricultural production has significantly increased. First, looking at the main grain, rice, production was 27.4 million bushels in 1970, but despite various disasters in 1979, it reached 38.6 million bushels, achieving a more than 40% increase. Furthermore, the production of meat such as beef, pork, and chicken, which was only 1.65 million tons in 1970, increased to 3.95 million tons in 1979, a 2.4-fold increase. The production of various vegetables, which was 4.95 million tons in 1975, increased to 8.14 million tons in just 4 years by 1979. When considering the driving force behind such a dramatic increase in our country's agricultural production, more than half of the credit should be given to the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement). This is because the movement provided the opportunity to overcome the deteriorating agricultural conditions in our country from various aspects.

Looking at the deterioration of agricultural conditions in concrete terms, farmland decreased for urbanization and industrialization, and the rural population decreased from 14.42 million in 1970 to 10.88 million in 1979, a decrease of about 30%. On the other hand, before the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) began in the 1960s, our rural areas were steeped in conservative and exclusive ways of thinking centered around "me" and "my family," and the consciousness of community and togetherness was very weak. Moreover, farming methods were centered around the family, with individual production and sales, far removed from collective production and sales.

However, since the Saemaul Undong (New Community Movement) began in 1970, our rural areas have started to change into a completely new appearance. First, improvements in the rural living environment such as roof improvement, farm road construction, and bridge construction were actively carried out through cooperative methods involving the entire village. This movement eventually developed into an increase production movement.


--- (p. 438) ---
